title: Pseudo-classes and Pseudo-elements
description: Selecting element state with :hover/:focus-visible/:nth-child, and generated content with ::before/::after.

blocks.content: Pseudo-classes (single colon: `:hover`, `:focus-visible`, `:checked`, `:nth-child()`) select elements based on state or structural position that plain selectors can't express. Pseudo-elements (double colon: `::before`, `::after`, `::first-line`) target a generated sub-part of an element rather than the element itself — `::before`/`::after` create a box positioned inside the element, controlled by the `content` property.
keyPoints: `:focus-visible` matches only when the browser's heuristics determine focus should be visibly indicated (e.g. keyboard navigation) — unlike `:focus`, it generally doesn't trigger on mouse clicks, avoiding an outline ring on every button click while still showing it for keyboard users.
Content inside `::before`/`::after` is decorative and not part of the accessibility tree in most cases — never put essential text only inside generated content.
Never gate essential functionality behind `:hover` alone — touch devices have no true hover state, and keyboard-only users don't trigger it either.

blocks.explanation: The focus ring only appears for keyboard focus (not every mouse click), and the required-field asterisk is purely decorative — the actual 'required' semantics still need a real `required` attribute or `aria-required`, not just the visible asterisk.

blocks.question: Why is `:focus-visible` generally preferred over `:focus` for custom focus-ring styling in a modern app?
blocks.answer: `:focus` matches any time an element has focus, including after a mouse click — which is why many older sites disabled outlines entirely (`outline: none`) to avoid an ugly ring on every click, inadvertently breaking keyboard accessibility in the process. `:focus-visible` lets you restore a clear, deliberate focus ring specifically for keyboard/assistive-technology users without reintroducing the ring-on-every-click problem for mouse users.
blocks.explanation: This app's shared components use `:focus-visible` in the `focus-ring()` SCSS mixin for exactly this reason.

title: CSS Transitions and Animations
description: Animating property changes smoothly, and respecting the user's reduced-motion preference.

blocks.content: `transition` animates a property smoothly between its old and new value whenever that value changes (hover, class toggle, etc.) — it needs a starting and ending state but no intermediate steps defined. `@keyframes` + `animation` define an explicit, potentially multi-step, potentially looping sequence independent of any state change. Both should list specific properties (`transition: transform 150ms ease`) rather than `transition: all`, and both should respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.
keyPoints: Animating `transform` and `opacity` is comparatively cheap because browsers can often handle them on the compositor thread; animating `width`/`height`/`top`/`left` forces layout recalculation on every frame.
`transition: all` silently animates properties you didn't intend to (including ones added later by another rule), making performance and behavior harder to reason about.
`@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` lets you disable or shrink nonessential motion for users who've indicated they're sensitive to it at the OS level.

blocks.explanation: Only `transform` and `box-shadow` are listed explicitly (not `all`), and the whole transition is disabled outright for users who've asked the OS to reduce motion.

blocks.question: You add `transition: height 200ms` to an accordion panel that toggles between `height: 0` and `height: auto`. The collapse animates fine, but the expand jumps instantly instead of animating. Why?
blocks.answer: CSS transitions cannot animate to or from `auto` — the browser has no defined intermediate values between a fixed height and `auto`, so it just snaps. Common fixes: transition `max-height` to a value larger than the content will ever need (a common but imperfect hack), or measure the content's actual height in JS and transition to that explicit pixel value, or use the newer `interpolate-size: allow-keywords` / `calc-size()` where supported.
blocks.explanation: This is one of the most commonly hit CSS animation gotchas — transitions require two concrete, interpolatable values, and `auto` isn't one.

title: SCSS Mixins and Functions
description: Emitting reusable style blocks with @mixin/@include, and computing values with @function.

blocks.content: A `@mixin` packages a reusable block of CSS declarations (optionally parameterized, optionally accepting a content block via `@content`) that gets copy-pasted into every `@include` site at compile time. A `@function` computes and returns a single Sass value (used inside a property value) rather than emitting declarations — `@function` is to values what `@mixin` is to whole rule blocks.
keyPoints: Mixins can accept default parameter values (`@mixin focus-ring($width: 3px)`) so most call sites can omit arguments entirely.

`@content` inside a mixin lets the caller inject an arbitrary block of CSS into a specific spot — this is how this app's own `respond-to()` breakpoint mixin wraps caller-supplied styles in a `@media` query.

Because mixins are inlined at every `@include`, using the same parameterized mixin in hundreds of places can meaningfully bloat compiled CSS — functions don't have this problem since they only ever produce one value.

blocks.explanation: `respond-to()` is a mixin because it emits a whole `@media`-wrapped rule block via `@content`; `spacing()` is a function because it just computes one numeric value to plug into a property.

blocks.question: You need a helper that both (a) computes a spacing value for use in `calc()` expressions elsewhere, and (b) applies a full focus-ring style block. Would each be a mixin or a function?
blocks.answer: The spacing helper should be a `@function` (it returns one value you plug into other expressions). The focus-ring helper should be a `@mixin` (it emits multiple declarations — `outline`, `outline-offset`, possibly more — as a block via `@include`).
blocks.explanation: The rule of thumb: if you're going to write `property: helper(...)`, it's a function; if you're going to write `@include helper(...);` as its own statement producing one or more declarations, it's a mixin.

title: SCSS Maps, Loops and Partials
description: Structuring design tokens with maps, generating repetitive styles with @each/@for, and splitting files with @use.

blocks.content: A Sass map (`$breakpoints: (mobile: 480px, tablet: 768px, ...)`) is a key-value structure ideal for design tokens like breakpoints, spacing scales, or color palettes, looked up with `map.get()`. `@each` and `@for` loops can generate families of related rules (utility classes, numbered spacing steps) from a map or range instead of writing them by hand. Modern Sass code loads files with `@use`/`@forward` (namespaced, loaded once) rather than the legacy global `@import`, which is deprecated.
keyPoints: `@use 'sass:map'` must be loaded to access map functions like `map.get()` and `map.has-key()` in modern Sass.
Loops that generate a large number of rules keep the *source* small but can make the *compiled* CSS output large — audit generated output size, don't assume terse source means terse CSS.
`@forward` re-exports a partial's members as part of a package's public API, letting a library present a single entry-point module to consumers.

blocks.explanation: The `@each` loop generates `.m-1`..`.m-4` and `.p-1`..`.p-4` utility classes from a single map definition, and `space()` gives component code a typed way to reuse the same scale in arbitrary property values.

blocks.question: Why does modern Sass tooling recommend `@use` over the older `@import`, beyond just namespacing?
blocks.answer: `@import` is fully global — every variable, mixin, and function from an imported file pollutes the same global namespace and can silently collide with anything else imported anywhere in the app, and a file imported multiple times gets re-evaluated (and its CSS re-emitted) each time. `@use` loads a module exactly once no matter how many files `@use` it, requires an explicit namespace prefix (`tokens.$spacing`) to access its members (eliminating naming collisions), and is what `@forward` is built on for building clean public APIs.
blocks.explanation: `@import` is formally deprecated in Dart Sass and scheduled for eventual removal — new SCSS code should default to `@use`/`@forward`.

title: Semantic HTML for an enterprise dashboard
description: Senior/lead scenario: A dashboard is built almost entirely with div elements and click handlers. What would you change?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Semantic HTML means choosing tags for meaning, not for appearance. A button is not just a rectangle with a click handler; it also carries keyboard behavior, focus behavior, and a role that assistive technology understands.

Dashboards often have repeated regions, dense data, filters, and actions. Good structure helps everyone move through that information faster.

ARIA can help in some cases, but native elements should do most of the work. The simpler the markup, the less behavior the team has to rebuild and maintain.
keyPoints: Use native landmarks and elements that match meaning: header, nav, main, section, aside, button, table, form, label, and heading hierarchy.
Native semantics improve keyboard behavior, accessibility APIs, search understanding, and maintainability without extra JavaScript.
Use buttons for actions and links for navigation. Do not simulate them with clickable divs unless a native element truly cannot meet the requirement.
Create one logical page heading structure and descriptive region labels for repeated sections.
Validate the accessibility tree and navigate with keyboard and screen reader, not only visual inspection.

blocks.question: A dashboard is built almost entirely with div elements and click handlers. What would you change?
blocks.answer:
I would replace the clickable div soup with elements that already mean what the UI is doing: header, nav, main, section, aside, form, label, button, link, and table where the data is tabular.

Actions should be buttons. Navigation should be links. That alone gives users keyboard behavior, expected browser behavior, and better accessibility support without extra code.

I would give the page a clear heading structure so people can scan it, including people using screen readers. Repeated areas like filters, alerts, and activity panels should have useful region names.

For dashboard data, I would use tables when users compare rows and columns. If the UI has custom controls inside the table, each control still needs a clear name.

After the markup change, I would check the page by tabbing through it and reviewing what assistive tech exposes, because a dashboard can look fine while still being impossible to operate.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Native elements may need extra styling to match a dense enterprise design, but that styling is cheaper than rebuilding browser behavior. The main risk is breaking existing click analytics or CSS hooks during migration, so I would convert by component and monitor keyboard completion, error rates, and accessibility defects after release.
keyPoints: Test keyboard, screen reader, touch, 200%/400% zoom, narrow and wide containers, forced colors, reduced motion, localization, browser compatibility and performance budgets.

blocks.question: When is a div with role="button" still justified?
blocks.answer: A div with role="button" is justified only when a real button cannot be used, which is rare. If we use it, we must add keyboard support for Enter and Space, focus styling, disabled behavior if needed, and a clear accessible name. I would still ask why a native button fails before accepting that trade.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it does not ban ARIA blindly, but it treats custom behavior as a cost that must be fully paid.

title: Accessible form design
description: Senior/lead scenario: A form uses placeholder text instead of labels and shows errors only in red. How would you redesign it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A form should be understandable before, during, and after input. Labels tell users what the field is. Help text explains rules. Errors explain repair.

Programmatic connections matter because visual proximity is not enough for screen readers. The browser needs to know which label and message belong to which control.

Color is useful, but color alone is not enough. Some users will not see the red, and some environments change colors entirely.
keyPoints: Provide persistent programmatic labels associated with controls. Placeholder text can supplement a label but should not replace it.
Connect help and error text using aria-describedby, set invalid state appropriately, and move or announce focus to the error summary after submission.
Use text and icons in addition to color. Error messages should explain what is wrong and how to fix it.
Group related controls with fieldset and legend where appropriate and preserve logical tab order.
Support autocomplete tokens for common personal data and test zoom, keyboard, and screen-reader behavior.

blocks.question: A form uses placeholder text instead of labels and shows errors only in red. How would you redesign it?
blocks.answer:
I would add real labels that stay visible. Placeholder text can give an example, but it disappears and is not a reliable label.

Each input should be connected to its label in code. Help text and error text should also be connected, usually with aria-describedby, so the user hears the right context.

Errors should not be red only. I would include clear text like Enter a valid email address, plus an icon or other shape if useful. The message should say what went wrong and how to fix it.

On submit, I would show an error summary near the top and move focus there when the form fails. From there, users can jump to each broken field.

For grouped controls like radio buttons, I would use fieldset and legend. I would also add autocomplete tokens for common personal data so the browser can help users fill the form faster.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: More visible labels and error summaries take space, but they reduce failed submissions and support more users. I would validate this in production by watching form completion, validation loops, abandoned submits, and support tickets for confusing fields.

blocks.question: How would you announce an asynchronous server validation error?
blocks.answer: For an async server error, I would attach the new error message to the field and set the field as invalid. If the user is still on that field, I would announce the message through a polite live region or update the described text so it is read. If the validation blocks submission, the error summary should include it too.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it handles both field-level context and the moment when the server result arrives.

title: Keyboard navigation in a custom data grid
description: Senior/lead scenario: A custom grid supports mouse selection but keyboard users cannot operate it. What behavior would you design?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A custom grid is not accessible because it has role=grid. It is accessible only if the behavior matches what that role promises.

Tables and grids solve different problems. A table is for reading relationships. A grid is closer to a spreadsheet or file picker, where users move around and change selection.

Virtualization adds another layer because the browser only sees part of the data. The UI must keep focus, position, and state stable even while rows are swapped in and out.
keyPoints: Decide whether it is truly an interactive ARIA grid or a semantic table with controls. Do not add grid roles without implementing the required interaction model.
Provide predictable arrow-key or tab behavior, a single managed tab stop where appropriate, and visible focus.
Expose row/column headers, selected and expanded state, sort state, and accessible names for cell actions.
Support Home/End and page navigation only if the pattern and user need justify them.
Virtualization must preserve announced row counts, positions, and focus when DOM rows are recycled.

blocks.question: A custom grid supports mouse selection but keyboard users cannot operate it. What behavior would you design?
blocks.answer:
First I would decide whether this is really an interactive grid or just a table with a few controls. If users only read and compare data, a normal table is usually better.

If it is an interactive grid, then it needs a complete keyboard model. That means predictable arrow key movement, visible focus, and usually one tab stop into the grid instead of tabbing through every cell.

The grid should expose headers, row and column position, selection, expansion, and sort state. Cell buttons need clear names like Open invoice 123, not just Open.

I would support Home, End, Page Up, and Page Down only if the grid is large enough and users benefit from those shortcuts. Extra keys should not be added just to look advanced.

If rows are virtualized, focus must not get lost when DOM nodes are recycled. The announced row count and current position should still make sense.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: A rich grid can be powerful, but it is expensive to build and test. I would track keyboard usage, grid errors, abandoned tasks, and accessibility bug reports, and I would test large data sets because focus bugs often appear only with virtualization.
keyPoints: Test keyboard, screen reader, touch, 200%/400% zoom, narrow and wide containers, forced colors, reduced motion, localization, browser compatibility and performance budgets.

blocks.question: When is a normal table more accessible than an ARIA grid?
blocks.answer: A normal table is more accessible when the data is mostly read-only and users need to compare rows and columns. It gives screen readers table navigation, headers, and structure without forcing the team to implement a spreadsheet-like keyboard model. Adding grid roles in that case can make the experience harder, not better.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it chooses the simpler pattern when the interaction does not require a full grid.

title: Focus management in dialogs
description: Senior/lead scenario: A modal opens but screen-reader focus remains behind it. What are the correct focus behaviors?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A modal is a temporary context switch. Focus management tells the browser and the user that the active task has moved from the page into the dialog.

The core rules are simple: enter the dialog, stay inside while it is active, understand what it is, then return to the prior context.

The hard parts are destructive actions, nested dialogs, mobile screen readers, and cases where the trigger disappears after the action completes.
keyPoints: Move focus to a meaningful element inside the dialog, usually the heading, first field, or least destructive action depending on the task.
Trap keyboard focus within the modal while it is active and make background content inert or otherwise unavailable to assistive technology.
Provide an accessible name and description and support Escape unless closing would cause data loss requiring confirmation.
On close, return focus to the triggering element or a logical successor if it no longer exists.
Avoid nested modal stacks where possible and test browser zoom and mobile screen readers.

blocks.question: A modal opens but screen-reader focus remains behind it. What are the correct focus behaviors?
blocks.answer:
When the modal opens, focus should move into it. The best target depends on the job: the heading for a message, the first field for a short form, or a safe action when the dialog is destructive.

While the modal is open, Tab and Shift+Tab should stay inside it. Background content should not be reachable by keyboard or exposed as active content to assistive tech.

The dialog needs a clear name, usually from its heading, and a useful description when the text matters. Escape should close it unless closing would lose user work and needs confirmation.

When the dialog closes, focus should return to the button or link that opened it. If that element is gone, focus should move to the next sensible place in the workflow.

I would avoid stacking multiple modals if possible, because each layer makes focus and recovery harder.

blocks.question: Why can automatically focusing the first input be harmful in some dialogs?
blocks.answer: Focusing the first input can be harmful when the dialog starts with important instructions or when the first field opens a keyboard on mobile and hides the message. It can also be risky in destructive dialogs, where focus should not land on an action that users might trigger by accident.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it picks focus based on the task, not a fixed rule.

title: ARIA usage and misuse
description: Senior/lead scenario: A developer adds many ARIA roles to fix accessibility quickly. What guidance do you give?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
ARIA is a contract. When you add a role, you are telling assistive technology that the component behaves like that role.

Bad ARIA can make a good native element worse. It can hide useful text, announce the wrong control type, or promise keyboard behavior that does not exist.

Good accessibility usually starts with less code: correct elements, correct labels, and small ARIA additions where the platform needs help.
keyPoints: Prefer native HTML because it includes semantics and behavior. ARIA changes accessibility semantics but usually does not add keyboard behavior or visual state.
Use roles, states, and relationships only when they match the implemented interaction pattern.
Do not override correct native semantics unnecessarily, and avoid invalid role/element combinations.
Keep aria-label from replacing visible text when visible text can be associated directly.
Test the computed accessibility tree and real assistive technology output.

blocks.question: A developer adds many ARIA roles to fix accessibility quickly. What guidance do you give?
blocks.answer:
I would tell the developer to slow down and use native HTML first. ARIA can change what assistive technology hears, but it usually does not add keyboard behavior or visual behavior.

If something can be a button, make it a button. If it can be a label, use a label. Then ARIA is needed only for gaps like expanded state, relationships, or names that native HTML cannot express by itself.

Every role must match the actual behavior. A custom combobox, tab list, or grid needs the keyboard pattern and state model users expect from that role.

I would remove ARIA that fights the native element, such as overriding a real button with a strange role. I would also avoid hiding visible text behind aria-label when the visible text can be used directly.

The final check is the accessibility tree and real output, not just whether an automated scanner is quiet.

blocks.content: ARIA is useful for complex widgets, but it increases implementation and test responsibility. I would watch accessibility regressions by component, run targeted manual checks for custom widgets, and treat ARIA patterns as reusable library work instead of one-off fixes.

blocks.question: What does the principle "No ARIA is better than bad ARIA" mean in practice?
blocks.answer: No ARIA is better than bad ARIA means an ordinary native control is often safer than a custom control with wrong roles and missing behavior. Bad ARIA can actively mislead users, while plain HTML may still be understandable and operable. The goal is not to avoid ARIA; it is to use it only when it accurately describes the component.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it explains the user harm caused by incorrect semantics.

title: Color contrast and design tokens
description: Senior/lead scenario: A new theme passes visual review but fails contrast in disabled, hover, and error states. How would you prevent this?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Design tokens work best when they describe purpose. A semantic token lets the system change color values without every component knowing the palette.

Contrast problems often appear in states, not in the happy-path screenshot. Disabled, hover, focus, and error colors can look subtle in design review but fail for users.

Validation should happen at the token level and at the component level because a color can pass in one pairing and fail in another.
keyPoints: Define semantic color tokens for text, surface, border, focus, success, warning, and error states rather than using raw palette values throughout components.
Test token combinations against required contrast targets, including interactive states and non-text graphical indicators.
Do not communicate state using color alone; add text, icon shape, underline, or pattern as appropriate.
Include dark theme, high-contrast/forced-colors mode, and user-selected themes in automated and manual checks.
Make contrast validation part of design-system CI so product teams inherit safe defaults.

blocks.question: A new theme passes visual review but fails contrast in disabled, hover, and error states. How would you prevent this?
blocks.answer:
I would move the theme away from raw color values in components and into semantic tokens. Components should ask for text color, surface color, border color, focus color, and error color, not blue-500 or gray-300.

Then I would test the allowed token pairs for contrast across normal, hover, focus, disabled, success, warning, and error states. Non-text indicators like borders and icons need contrast too.

State should not depend on color alone. An error needs text. A selected item may need a checkmark, border, or label. A link needs more than just a color shift if the context is unclear.

Dark mode, forced-colors mode, and user themes should be part of the same token system. Product teams should inherit safe combinations instead of inventing new ones.

I would put contrast checks into design-system CI so broken token combinations fail early.

blocks.question: Why are disabled controls a special contrast and usability discussion?
blocks.answer: Disabled controls are tricky because they are intentionally lower emphasis, but users still need to know they exist and why they are unavailable. Some contrast rules treat disabled controls differently, but low contrast can still be a usability problem. I would pair the disabled styling with clear layout, labels, and help text when the reason matters.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it separates formal contrast rules from real usability.

title: Responsive design for a dense banking dashboard
description: Senior/lead scenario: A desktop dashboard has 12 cards, filters, charts, and a wide table. How would you make it usable on tablets and phones?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Responsive design is about changing the layout to protect the task. It is not about making every desktop pixel smaller.

Dense dashboards need priority. Some information is primary, some is supporting, and some can move into a later step.

Tables, filters, and charts often need different responsive patterns. One breakpoint cannot solve every component.
keyPoints: Prioritize tasks and information rather than shrinking the desktop layout. Identify what must remain visible, what can stack, and what can move into progressive disclosure.
Use fluid grid/flex layouts and component-level container queries where components live in varying widths.
Convert wide tables into horizontal scroll with sticky key columns, card/detail views, or a column chooser based on the workflow.
Keep touch targets, focus order, labels, and chart alternatives usable. Do not hide critical actions only on small screens.
Test real content, long localization strings, 200-400% zoom, landscape, and device safe areas.

blocks.question: A desktop dashboard has 12 cards, filters, charts, and a wide table. How would you make it usable on tablets and phones?
blocks.answer:
I would not try to shrink the desktop dashboard into a phone screen. I would start by ranking the main tasks: checking balances, spotting risk, filtering transactions, comparing accounts, or exporting data.

Cards can stack and some secondary cards can move behind disclosure. Filters may become a panel or sheet, but critical filters and active filter state must stay easy to find.

For the wide table, I would choose the pattern based on the work. Comparison may need horizontal scroll with sticky key columns. Row review may work better as a summary card with a details view.

Charts need simpler labels, useful summaries, and a way to inspect values without hover. Touch targets and focus order should still feel natural.

I would test with real banking content: long account names, many currencies, localized labels, zoom, landscape, and safe areas on mobile devices.

blocks.content: A weak answer is to hide half the cards and columns with CSS at small widths. That may make the page fit while removing the information users came for.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Progressive disclosure reduces clutter, but it can also bury useful comparisons. I would monitor mobile task completion, filter usage, horizontal scroll behavior, table detail opens, and support complaints about missing data.
keyPoints: Test keyboard, screen reader, touch, 200%/400% zoom, narrow and wide containers, forced colors, reduced motion, localization, browser compatibility and performance budgets.

blocks.question: How would you decide which table columns remain visible on mobile?
blocks.answer: I would keep columns that identify the row and support the top mobile task, such as account, amount, status, and date. Columns used less often can move into details, a column chooser, or a saved view. I would confirm the choice with usage data and business workflows, not just screen width.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it bases the column choice on user work and data importance.

title: Mobile-first versus desktop-first CSS
description: Senior/lead scenario: A legacy stylesheet uses many max-width overrides. Would you rewrite it mobile-first?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Mobile-first CSS means the default layout works in the most constrained space. Enhancements are layered on as more room is available.

The idea is useful, but the migration strategy matters. A risky full rewrite can create more problems than it solves.

Container queries change the discussion because components often live in sidebars, dialogs, and grids where viewport width is not the right signal.
keyPoints: Mobile-first starts with the simplest constrained layout and adds capability as space increases, often reducing override complexity.
A full rewrite is not automatically justified. Measure cascade complexity, regression risk, browser support, and expected component lifetime.
Migrate by component using logical base styles and min-width enhancements, while preserving visual-regression coverage.
Choose breakpoints based on content failure, not named devices.
Container queries can reduce dependence on global viewport breakpoints for reusable components.

blocks.question: A legacy stylesheet uses many max-width overrides. Would you rewrite it mobile-first?
blocks.answer:
Mobile-first is usually a good direction because the base style starts simple. Then larger screens add columns, spacing, and richer layout with min-width queries.

But I would not rewrite a legacy stylesheet just because mobile-first sounds cleaner. I would look at how tangled the cascade is, how many regressions a rewrite could cause, and how long the components will live.

For an active product, I would migrate component by component. Each component gets a flexible base layout, then larger-container enhancements.

Breakpoints should come from where content breaks, not from phone or tablet names. A card might need a different threshold than a navigation bar.

For reusable components, I would consider container queries so the component responds to its own space instead of the whole viewport.

blocks.title: Practical code / design example
blocks.explanation: Start with the constrained experience, then add layout capability as space becomes available.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.content: A weak answer is to convert every max-width query to min-width in one large pass without understanding the cascade. That is likely to create visual regressions everywhere.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Mobile-first can simplify future CSS, but migration can be noisy in a legacy app. I would validate with visual regression coverage, CSS size trends, defect rates by component, and production viewport or container-width analytics.
keyPoints: Test keyboard, screen reader, touch, 200%/400% zoom, narrow and wide containers, forced colors, reduced motion, localization, browser compatibility and performance budgets.

blocks.question: When can desktop-first be the more practical incremental choice?
blocks.answer: Desktop-first can be more practical when a stable desktop product only needs a few targeted small-screen fixes. It can also make sense during a gradual migration, where changing the base styles would disturb many routes. The important part is to stop adding random overrides and create a clear path forward.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it values maintainability and risk, not a slogan.

title: CSS Grid versus Flexbox
description: Senior/lead scenario: A developer asks whether to use Grid or Flexbox for every layout. How do you decide?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Flexbox is one-dimensional. It distributes space along one main axis and handles wrapping reasonably well.

Grid is two-dimensional. It lets rows and columns share a structure, which is useful when alignment across both directions matters.

Modern CSS layouts often combine both. The skill is knowing which part of the layout needs which model.
keyPoints: Flexbox is primarily one-dimensional and excels at distributing and aligning items along a row or column.
Grid is two-dimensional and excels when rows and columns must coordinate or content must align across tracks.
They work together: grid can define page/card tracks while flex aligns content inside each component.
Use intrinsic sizing functions such as minmax, auto-fit, and min-content carefully and test overflow with real data.
Choose based on layout relationships rather than browser myths or personal preference.

blocks.question: A developer asks whether to use Grid or Flexbox for every layout. How do you decide?
blocks.answer:
I decide based on the relationship in the layout. If items mainly need to line up in one direction, like a toolbar or a row of actions, Flexbox is usually the right tool.

If rows and columns need to work together, Grid is usually better. Page shells, card galleries, dashboards, and forms often benefit from grid tracks.

They are not competitors. I often use Grid for the outer structure and Flexbox inside a card or button group for alignment.

I would be careful with intrinsic sizing like minmax, auto-fit, min-content, and max-content. They are powerful, but real content can overflow in surprising ways.

The choice should come from the layout problem, not browser myths or personal preference.

blocks.code:
.toolbar { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: .75rem; flex-wrap: wrap; }
.dashboard { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(16rem, 1fr)); gap: 1rem; }
blocks.explanation: Flexbox is one-dimensional; Grid controls rows and columns together.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.content: A weak answer is to say Grid is newer so it should be used for everything. That ignores simple one-axis layouts where Flexbox is clearer.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Grid can make structure explicit, but overusing it for tiny alignment jobs can add complexity. I would validate with real content, long strings, zoom, and production layout bug reports tied to overflow or wrapping.
keyPoints: Test keyboard, screen reader, touch, 200%/400% zoom, narrow and wide containers, forced colors, reduced motion, localization, browser compatibility and performance budgets.

blocks.question: Why can min-width: 0 be necessary for a flex or grid child?
blocks.answer: min-width: 0 can be necessary because flex and grid children often refuse to shrink below their content's intrinsic width. A long word, URL, or table can force the whole layout wider than the container. Setting min-width: 0 tells the child it may shrink and let its content wrap, clip, or scroll as designed.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it explains the real overflow bug behind a common CSS fix.

title: Container queries
description: Senior/lead scenario: A card appears in a full-width page, a narrow sidebar, and a dialog. Viewport media queries produce wrong layouts. What would you use?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Viewport media queries ask how wide the browser is. Container queries ask how much room a component has.

That matters for reusable components. The same card may be wide on a page, narrow in a sidebar, and medium in a modal.

Container queries work best when the base design is solid and the enhancements are tied to real layout changes, not arbitrary device names.
keyPoints: Make the card’s parent a query container and adapt the card based on available container width rather than viewport width.
Use container queries for component composition and media queries for page/device-level concerns such as reduced motion or coarse pointers.
Define sensible intrinsic base styles so unsupported or unexpected contexts remain usable.
Avoid too many tiny thresholds that create hard-to-test layout states.
Document containment because it can affect sizing and layout behavior.

blocks.question: A card appears in a full-width page, a narrow sidebar, and a dialog. Viewport media queries produce wrong layouts. What would you use?
blocks.answer:
I would make the card respond to the space it actually has, not the viewport. The parent can become a query container, and the card can switch layout based on container width.

The default card should still be usable in a narrow space. Then wider containers can add side-by-side media, extra metadata, or denser controls.

I would still use media queries for page-level or device-level concerns, like reduced motion, pointer type, or print. Container queries are for component layout in different placements.

I would avoid a long list of tiny thresholds. A few meaningful states are easier to design, test, and maintain.

I would document the container requirement because containment can affect sizing and surprise other developers.

blocks.explanation: A reusable component responds to its allocated space rather than the full viewport.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.content: A weak answer is to add more viewport breakpoints until the card looks right in three screenshots. That still fails when the card appears in a new container size.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Container queries make components more portable, but too many variants can become hard to reason about. I would track component placements, visual regressions by container size, and production errors where content overflows in sidebars or dialogs.
keyPoints: Test keyboard, screen reader, touch, 200%/400% zoom, narrow and wide containers, forced colors, reduced motion, localization, browser compatibility and performance budgets.

blocks.question: What is the difference between size, style, and scroll-state container queries?
blocks.answer: Size container queries react to the container's dimensions. Style queries react to computed style values, such as a custom property. Scroll-state queries react to scroll-related states, like whether a container is stuck or scrollable, where supported.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it distinguishes the trigger for each query type in plain terms.

title: Fluid typography
description: Senior/lead scenario: Design wants text to scale smoothly between mobile and desktop. How would you implement it safely?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Fluid typography lets text change gradually as space changes. clamp is a safe pattern because it gives the browser boundaries.

The accessible version does not hand all control to viewport width. Users still need their font preferences and zoom to work.

Typography is not only size. Line length, wrapping, hierarchy, and localization all decide whether the result is readable.
keyPoints: Use clamp with a minimum, fluid preferred value, and maximum rather than many abrupt breakpoints.
Keep values based on rem plus a controlled viewport component so browser text zoom remains effective.
Validate line length, wrapping, headings, and localization at all intermediate widths.
Do not allow decorative scaling to violate minimum readable sizes or create extreme headings.
Test user font-size settings and 200% zoom.

blocks.question: Design wants text to scale smoothly between mobile and desktop. How would you implement it safely?
blocks.answer:
I would use clamp so each text style has a minimum, a fluid middle value, and a maximum. That gives smooth scaling without a pile of breakpoints.

The formula should include rem, not only viewport units. That keeps browser text settings and zoom useful for people who need larger text.

I would set limits for readability. Body text should not become tiny on mobile, and headings should not become huge just because the viewport is wide.

Then I would test line length, wrapping, headings, and translated strings across the range. Smooth scaling can still create awkward breaks.

I would include 200% zoom and larger default font settings in the checks, because type that looks elegant at normal size can fail quickly.

blocks.code:
h1 { font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 1.2rem + 2vw, 3rem); line-height: 1.15; }
body { font-size: 1rem; line-height: 1.5; }
blocks.explanation: Clamp keeps text fluid within tested minimum and maximum sizes.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.content: A weak answer is to set all headings in vw and call the page responsive. That may look fluid while failing zoom and readability.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Fluid type reduces breakpoint jumps, but it can make design QA harder because every width is a possible state. I would validate with typography snapshots, localization checks, zoom testing, and production reports of clipped headings or unreadable text.
keyPoints: Test keyboard, screen reader, touch, 200%/400% zoom, narrow and wide containers, forced colors, reduced motion, localization, browser compatibility and performance budgets.

blocks.question: Why can pure vw font sizing be an accessibility problem?
blocks.answer: Pure vw sizing can ignore the user's preferred font size because it is tied only to the viewport. It can also make text too small on narrow screens or too large on wide displays. Mixing rem with a controlled viewport part gives smoother scaling while keeping user control.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it connects the CSS choice to user-controlled text size.

title: Preventing cumulative layout shift
description: Senior/lead scenario: A page jumps while images, ads, and async widgets load. How would you reduce CLS?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
CLS measures unexpected movement while the page is loading or updating. Users lose their place, click the wrong thing, or feel that the page is unstable.

The fix is usually to make space predictable. Late content should fill a planned slot instead of pushing the page around.

Lab tools help, but production data matters because third-party scripts and slow paths create shifts that test machines may not capture.
keyPoints: Reserve dimensions for images, video, embeds, charts, and skeletons using width/height, aspect-ratio, or stable containers.
Do not insert banners above existing content after load unless space was reserved or the user triggered the change.
Preload critical fonts appropriately and use font metrics/fallback strategies to reduce text reflow.
Keep placeholders close to final dimensions and avoid replacing a one-line loader with a large unknown panel.
Use real-user CLS attribution because lab data may not capture late interaction shifts.

blocks.question: A page jumps while images, ads, and async widgets load. How would you reduce CLS?
blocks.answer:
I would reserve space for anything that loads later: images, video, ads, charts, embeds, and large widgets. Width, height, aspect-ratio, or a stable wrapper can prevent the page from jumping.

I would not insert banners or promos above existing content after load unless space was already reserved or the user caused the change.

For fonts, I would preload only what is critical and choose fallback metrics that are close to the final font. That reduces text reflow when the real font arrives.

Skeletons should be close to the final layout. Replacing a tiny spinner with a large panel is still a layout shift.

I would use real-user CLS attribution because late shifts from ads, consent banners, or slow widgets often do not show up in a clean lab run.

blocks.explanation: Weak version to avoid: A weak answer is to optimize image file size only. Smaller images may load faster, but the page can still jump if their dimensions are unknown.

blocks.title: Practical code / design example
blocks.explanation: Reserve space for media and async components before they load.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.content: A weak answer is to optimize image file size only. Smaller images may load faster, but the page can still jump if their dimensions are unknown.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Reserving space can leave temporary empty areas, but it protects stability. I would validate with Core Web Vitals field data, route-level CLS attribution, ad/widget monitoring, and click-misfire reports.
keyPoints: Test keyboard, screen reader, touch, 200%/400% zoom, narrow and wide containers, forced colors, reduced motion, localization, browser compatibility and performance budgets.

blocks.question: How can a cookie banner be designed without causing a large layout shift?
blocks.answer: A cookie banner can avoid a big shift by using a reserved region, an overlay that does not move page content, or a bottom bar that is accounted for in the layout. It should not suddenly push the whole page down after the user starts reading. The choice should still keep controls reachable and not cover critical actions.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it solves the shift while still considering usability of the banner itself.

title: Critical CSS and loading strategy
description: Senior/lead scenario: The page downloads a large global stylesheet before rendering. Would you inline critical CSS?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Critical CSS is about getting the first useful pixels styled quickly. It is not a reason to paste the whole stylesheet into HTML.

Inlining trades cacheability for early rendering. That trade can help first visits and hurt repeat navigation if it is overdone.

The safest setup is automated, measured, and tied to the build pipeline so the inlined CSS stays in sync.
keyPoints: Inline only the small styles required for initial above-the-fold rendering and load the remaining stylesheet normally.
Keep critical extraction automated and consistent with the deployed HTML; stale critical CSS can cause flashes or duplication.
Use caching wisely: too much inline CSS increases HTML size and repeats on every page.
Split CSS by route/component where tooling supports it and remove unused framework/theme payloads.
Measure first content, style recalculation, transfer, and cache reuse rather than applying a generic optimization.

blocks.question: The page downloads a large global stylesheet before rendering. Would you inline critical CSS?
blocks.answer:
I would consider inlining critical CSS, but only the small set needed to render the first view. The rest of the stylesheet should still load normally and be cached.

The critical CSS must be generated from the same build as the deployed page. Stale critical CSS can cause flashes, duplicate rules, or styles that no longer match the HTML.

I would also look for easier wins: route-level CSS splitting, removing unused framework styles, and cutting theme payload that the page does not need.

Too much inline CSS makes every HTML response heavier. That can hurt repeat visits where a cached stylesheet would have been cheaper.

I would measure first render, transfer size, style recalculation, cache reuse, and route behavior before making the optimization permanent.

blocks.code:
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/app.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/app.css">
blocks.explanation: Inline only truly critical styles, cache the main stylesheet, and avoid excessive font variants.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.content: A weak answer is to inline the entire global stylesheet. That may remove one request but bloats every page and can make caching worse.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Critical CSS can improve first paint, but it adds build complexity and stale-style risk. I would validate with synthetic and real-user metrics, HTML weight, cache hit behavior, and visual reports of flashes or unstyled content.
keyPoints: Test keyboard, screen reader, touch, 200%/400% zoom, narrow and wide containers, forced colors, reduced motion, localization, browser compatibility and performance budgets.

blocks.question: When can inlining critical CSS make repeat navigation worse?
blocks.answer: Inlining critical CSS can hurt repeat navigation when the same styles are sent again inside every HTML page instead of being reused from a cached stylesheet. If the inline block grows large, users pay that cost on each page. It can also delay HTML parsing if the server sends too much CSS upfront.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it explains the cache trade-off instead of treating inlining as always faster.

title: CSS specificity conflict
description: Senior/lead scenario: Teams keep adding !important and longer selectors to override each other. How would you fix the cascade?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Specificity problems are often ownership problems. If no one knows which rule is supposed to win, teams keep making selectors stronger.

Cascade layers let a project define broad priority before selector specificity is considered inside a layer. That makes source order and ownership easier to reason about.

Good component APIs also matter. Teams should not need deep selectors to make supported changes.
keyPoints: Establish layers for reset, tokens, base, components, utilities, and overrides so source order and ownership are explicit.
Keep component selectors shallow and class-based. Avoid styling through deep DOM structure or IDs.
Use :where for intentionally zero-specificity wrappers and expose component states through classes/data attributes.
Remove global selectors that leak into product components and migrate exceptions into documented APIs.
Use developer tools to inspect the winning declaration rather than adding another override blindly.

blocks.question: Teams keep adding !important and longer selectors to override each other. How would you fix the cascade?
blocks.answer:
I would stop the override race by making the cascade explicit. A layer order for reset, tokens, base, components, utilities, and product overrides gives teams a shared model.

Component selectors should stay shallow and mostly class-based. Deep selectors and IDs make later changes harder and encourage more important flags.

For low-specificity wrappers, I would use :where where it helps. For component states, I would expose classes or data attributes instead of asking teams to target internal DOM.

Then I would remove or contain global selectors that leak into product components. Exceptions should become documented APIs, not random overrides.

When debugging, I would inspect the winning declaration in DevTools before writing another selector.

blocks.explanation: Keep selectors shallow and make precedence intentional instead of escalating with IDs and !important.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Layers and shallow selectors improve predictability, but migration can expose hidden dependencies. I would validate with CSS linting, visual regression tests, override counts, and production style bugs by owning team.

blocks.question: How do cascade layers change the importance of selector specificity?
blocks.answer: Cascade layers make layer order more important than selector specificity for normal author styles. A low-specificity rule in a later layer can beat a high-specificity rule in an earlier layer. Specificity still matters between rules inside the same layer.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it states exactly where specificity still applies.

title: Cascade layers
description: Senior/lead scenario: A design system must coexist with legacy CSS and product overrides. How can @layer help?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Cascade layers are a way to organize priority in CSS. They answer the question: which category of rule should win before we argue about selector strength?

They are useful when a design system must coexist with legacy CSS, vendor CSS, and product-specific overrides.

The layer contract needs documentation. If teams do not know where their styles belong, the cascade becomes confusing again.
keyPoints: Declare an explicit layer order so lower-priority legacy/base rules cannot unexpectedly beat component or utility rules regardless of selector strength within normal origin rules.
Place third-party styles in a known low-priority layer when build tooling permits and keep product overrides in a deliberate layer.
Unlayered author styles can outrank layered normal styles, so adoption must be planned rather than partial and accidental.
Layers do not replace good component APIs or remove the need to control !important.
Document the layer contract for consumers.

blocks.question: A design system must coexist with legacy CSS and product overrides. How can @layer help?
blocks.answer:
@layer can help by giving the design system and legacy CSS a clear priority order. For example, reset and legacy rules can sit below base, components, utilities, and deliberate product overrides.

That means an old high-specificity selector does not automatically beat a newer component rule if it is in a lower layer.

Third-party CSS can also be placed in a known low-priority layer when the build allows it. Product overrides should live in a named layer, not as random untracked CSS.

I would be careful with partial adoption. Unlayered author styles can outrank layered normal styles, so one unlayered file can break the model.

Layers do not remove the need for good component APIs or discipline around !important. They make the rules easier to enforce.

blocks.question: What happens when one stylesheet is unlayered while others are layered?
blocks.answer: Unlayered author styles usually outrank layered normal author styles. So if most of the app is layered but one stylesheet is not, that stylesheet may unexpectedly win. A rollout should either layer the important files deliberately or account for that behavior.

title: Stacking context and z-index
description: Senior/lead scenario: A tooltip has z-index: 999999 but still appears behind a transformed panel. Why?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Stacking order decides what paints on top within a context. A child cannot always escape its parent's stacking context just by having a larger number.

Overlays are easier to manage when they render in a known layer system. Otherwise every component invents a bigger z-index.

Clipping is a separate issue. An element can be on top and still be cut off by overflow.
keyPoints: z-index is compared within stacking contexts, not as one global number. Properties such as transform, opacity, isolation, positioned elements with z-index, and filters can create new contexts.
Inspect ancestor stacking contexts and move the overlay to an appropriate portal/root layer rather than escalating numbers.
Create a small z-index token scale for base, sticky, dropdown, modal, toast, and tooltip layers.
Account for clipping from overflow and containing blocks, which z-index alone cannot solve.
Test nested dialogs and fullscreen modes.

blocks.question: A tooltip has z-index: 999999 but still appears behind a transformed panel. Why?
blocks.answer:
The huge z-index is not working because z-index is not one global ladder. It is compared inside stacking contexts.

A transformed ancestor can create a new stacking context. So can opacity, filters, isolation, positioned elements with z-index, and other properties.

I would inspect the tooltip's ancestors and find which context traps it. If it is an overlay, it may need to render in a portal or shared overlay root instead of inside the transformed panel.

I would also check overflow clipping. If an ancestor clips its children, z-index cannot draw the tooltip outside that box.

Long term, I would use a small z-index token scale for layers like sticky, dropdown, modal, toast, and tooltip instead of random giant numbers.

blocks.question: How does overflow clipping differ from stacking order?
blocks.answer: Stacking order decides which element is painted in front when elements overlap. Overflow clipping decides whether content outside an ancestor's box is visible at all. If a parent has overflow hidden, a tooltip can be clipped even if its z-index is higher than nearby content.

title: CSS containment and content-visibility
description: Senior/lead scenario: A long page with many off-screen panels is expensive to render. Would you use CSS containment or content-visibility?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
CSS containment tells the browser that a section is isolated in certain ways. That can reduce how much work the browser does when something changes.

content-visibility: auto is useful for long pages because off-screen content can stay in the document while rendering work is delayed.

The trade is that containment changes assumptions. Features that depend on natural size or position may behave differently.
keyPoints: content-visibility: auto can skip rendering work for off-screen content while retaining it in the document, and contain-intrinsic-size can reserve approximate space.
Containment can isolate layout, paint, size, or style calculations, but it may change sizing and positioning behavior.
Use it for well-bounded sections and test find-in-page, focus navigation, accessibility, sticky positioning, and printing.
Do not use it as a substitute for data virtualization when the DOM and memory are still enormous.
Measure browser support and real rendering cost.

blocks.question: A long page with many off-screen panels is expensive to render. Would you use CSS containment or content-visibility?
blocks.answer:
I would consider content-visibility: auto for well-bounded off-screen sections. It lets the browser skip rendering work until the content is near the viewport.

I would pair it with contain-intrinsic-size so the page reserves an approximate height and does not jump badly when the section renders.

For containment, I would choose the type carefully. Layout, paint, size, and style containment can improve isolation, but they can also change sizing, positioning, and sticky behavior.

I would not use this as a replacement for virtualization if the DOM is massive. The browser may skip some rendering, but memory and DOM cost can still be too high.

I would test focus navigation, find-in-page, accessibility, printing, sticky elements, and actual rendering cost before rolling it out widely.

blocks.explanation: Skip off-screen rendering only after checking accessibility, find-in-page, and intrinsic-size behavior.

blocks.question: How can an incorrect intrinsic size cause scroll jumps?
blocks.answer: If the intrinsic size is too small or too large, the browser reserves the wrong amount of space before the real content renders. When the real size becomes known, the scroll position can shift. That feels like a jump even though the content was technically already in the document.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it explains why the placeholder size matters to scroll stability.

title: Animating without jank
description: Senior/lead scenario: A sidebar animation triggers layout on every frame. How would you improve it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Jank happens when the browser cannot finish work before the next frame. Layout and paint are often more expensive than compositing.

Transforms and opacity are not magic, but they are usually safer animation targets than changing geometry in a large layout.

Animation quality includes accessibility. A smooth animation can still be wrong if it causes motion sickness or breaks focus.
keyPoints: Prefer transform and opacity for animations because they often avoid repeated layout and can be composited efficiently.
Avoid animating width, height, top, or left in large layouts unless measured and acceptable.
Keep duration and easing appropriate, and respect prefers-reduced-motion with a meaningful non-animated state.
Do not add will-change permanently to many elements; it consumes resources and should be targeted.
Profile frame time, paint, and layer count on lower-end devices.

blocks.question: A sidebar animation triggers layout on every frame. How would you improve it?
blocks.answer:
I would avoid animating layout-heavy properties like width, height, top, or left for the sidebar. Those can force layout and paint work on every frame.

If the design allows it, I would animate transform, such as translateX, and opacity. Those are more likely to run on the compositor and stay smooth.

The final open and closed states still need to be real layout states. The animation should not leave content unreachable or confuse focus order.

I would respect prefers-reduced-motion and provide a simple state change or very small fade for users who request less motion.

I would profile the animation on a lower-end device and watch frame time, paint, layout cost, and layer count. I would use will-change only around the animation, not permanently on many elements.

blocks.explanation: Weak version to avoid: A weak answer is to add will-change everywhere and hope the browser fixes it. That can waste memory and make performance worse.

blocks.title: Practical code / design example
blocks.code:
.drawer { transform: translateX(100%); transition: transform 180ms ease; }
.drawer[data-open="true"] { transform: translateX(0); }
blocks.explanation: Animate transform and opacity where possible; avoid repeated layout-triggering properties.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.content: A weak answer is to add will-change everywhere and hope the browser fixes it. That can waste memory and make performance worse.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Transform animations can keep frames smooth, but they may complicate layout, hit testing, and text rendering during movement. I would validate with performance traces, reduced-motion usage, interaction latency, and production reports of slow or stuck transitions.
keyPoints: Test keyboard, screen reader, touch, 200%/400% zoom, narrow and wide containers, forced colors, reduced motion, localization, browser compatibility and performance budgets.

blocks.question: When can transform animation still be expensive?
blocks.answer: Transform animation can still be expensive if the element is huge, has costly filters or shadows, contains video/canvas, or creates too many layers. It can also hurt memory on low-end devices. Composited does not mean free.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it avoids the oversimplification that transforms are always cheap.

title: Reduced motion
description: Senior/lead scenario: The application contains parallax, auto-scrolling banners, and animated charts. How do you support users who prefer reduced motion?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Reduced motion is a user preference, often set at the operating-system level. It helps people who experience dizziness, distraction, or discomfort from movement.

The goal is not to make the interface lifeless. The goal is to remove motion that is not needed for understanding.

A consistent token or motion system makes this easier because components can share durations, easing, and reduced variants.
keyPoints: Use prefers-reduced-motion to remove or greatly reduce non-essential movement and provide direct state changes or fades.
Do not disable useful progress feedback or state communication; simplify it.
Avoid auto-playing movement that cannot be paused, especially when it affects reading or causes vestibular discomfort.
Put motion tokens and reduced variants in the design system.
Test the complete workflow with the operating-system setting enabled.

blocks.question: The application contains parallax, auto-scrolling banners, and animated charts. How do you support users who prefer reduced motion?
blocks.answer:
I would use prefers-reduced-motion to remove or greatly reduce non-essential movement. Parallax and auto-scrolling banners are strong candidates to disable.

For animated charts, I would keep the information but simplify the motion. For example, show the final state directly or use a very short fade instead of sweeping bars across the screen.

I would not remove useful feedback. Loading, progress, and state changes still need to be clear; they just do not need dramatic motion.

Auto-playing movement should be pausable, especially if it competes with reading. If the motion is decorative, it should not run for users who asked for less.

I would put reduced-motion variants into the design system so each team does not invent its own interpretation.

blocks.title: Practical code / design example
blocks.explanation: Reduce non-essential motion while preserving necessary state changes.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.content: A weak answer is to turn off only the biggest homepage animation and leave banners, charts, and route transitions moving everywhere else.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Reduced variants may make some branded moments less dramatic, but they make the product safer to use. I would validate by testing workflows with the OS setting enabled and monitoring complaints, preference usage, and animation-related accessibility issues.

blocks.question: Should all animations become zero-duration when reduced motion is requested?
blocks.answer: No, reduced motion does not always mean zero-duration. Some small fades or instant state changes may be clearer than abrupt content jumps. The key is to remove large movement, parallax, zooming, and auto motion that can cause discomfort.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it keeps useful feedback while honoring the user's preference.

title: Dark mode architecture
description: Senior/lead scenario: Add dark mode to a large application without duplicating every stylesheet. What approach would you use?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Dark mode is not an inverted stylesheet. It is a theme system based on meaning.

Semantic tokens let a component say what role a color plays. Then each theme can provide suitable values for that role.

The hard parts are often assets and edge states: charts, disabled controls, focus rings, errors, shadows, and third-party widgets.
keyPoints: Define semantic design tokens as CSS custom properties and switch token values by theme on a root attribute or class.
Do not map components directly to palette numbers; use meanings such as surface, text, border, focus, and critical.
Use color-scheme so native controls and browser UI align where appropriate.
Persist explicit user choice, otherwise respect prefers-color-scheme, and prevent a flash of the wrong theme during startup.
Test contrast, images, charts, shadows, syntax highlighting, and forced-colors mode.

blocks.question: Add dark mode to a large application without duplicating every stylesheet. What approach would you use?
blocks.answer:
I would build dark mode through semantic tokens, usually CSS custom properties. Components should use tokens like surface, text, border, focus, and critical instead of hardcoded palette colors.

Theme switching can happen by changing a root class or data attribute that changes token values. That avoids duplicating every component stylesheet.

I would use color-scheme where appropriate so native controls, form fields, and browser UI can match the active theme.

User choice should be persisted. If the user has not chosen, the app can follow prefers-color-scheme. The startup path needs to set the theme early to avoid a flash of the wrong colors.

I would test more than backgrounds and text: images, icons, charts, shadows, syntax highlighting, contrast, and forced-colors mode all need attention.

blocks.title: Practical code / design example
blocks.explanation: Theme semantic tokens, not individual component colors, and test contrast in every state.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.content: A weak answer is to create a second dark copy of every stylesheet. That doubles maintenance and still misses hardcoded colors inside components.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Semantic tokens reduce duplication, but token migration can expose many hardcoded assumptions. I would validate with contrast checks, screenshot coverage by theme, field reports of theme flashes, and production tracking of user theme preference.
keyPoints: Test keyboard, screen reader, touch, 200%/400% zoom, narrow and wide containers, forced colors, reduced motion, localization, browser compatibility and performance budgets.

blocks.question: How would you avoid a theme flash before JavaScript loads?
blocks.answer: I would set the theme before the main app renders, using a small inline script or server-rendered attribute based on saved preference and system preference. The CSS should key off that early attribute. That way the first paint uses the right token values.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it handles the first paint, not just theme switching after JavaScript loads.

title: High-contrast and forced-colors mode
description: Senior/lead scenario: Custom controls disappear in Windows high-contrast mode. How would you fix them?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Forced-colors mode lets the user's system choose colors for readability. Custom UI often breaks because it assumes its own colors and images will remain visible.

System colors and native controls work with the mode instead of fighting it. Custom controls need explicit boundaries and states that do not depend on subtle color differences.

The goal is not to make high contrast look identical to the default theme. The goal is to keep the UI understandable and operable.
keyPoints: Use semantic native elements and system colors where possible so the browser can adapt controls.
Test forced-colors media behavior and avoid relying on background images or subtle box shadows as the only boundary.
Use forced-color-adjust only for targeted content where preserving original color is essential; do not disable user adaptation broadly.
Ensure focus, selected, error, and disabled states remain visible through borders, text, or system colors.
Include high-contrast testing in the design-system acceptance process.

blocks.question: Custom controls disappear in Windows high-contrast mode. How would you fix them?
blocks.answer:
I would first check whether the custom controls can use native elements or at least native semantics. Browsers do a lot of adaptation for real controls in forced-colors mode.

I would stop relying on background images, subtle shadows, or low-contrast fills as the only visible boundary. Borders, text, and system colors survive better.

Focus, selected, error, and disabled states must remain visible. A custom checkbox, for example, needs a shape or border that still appears when colors are forced.

I would use forced-color-adjust only in narrow cases where preserving original color is essential. Turning off user adaptation broadly defeats the user's setting.

This should become part of design-system acceptance, because one broken primitive can make many apps unusable.

blocks.title: Practical code / design example
blocks.explanation: Allow system colors to communicate state and verify that custom icons/borders remain visible.

blocks.content: A weak answer is to disable forced-colors adjustments for the whole app so the design looks closer to the mockup. That ignores the user's accessibility setting.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Forced-colors support may reduce brand-specific visuals, but it preserves usability. I would validate with Windows forced-colors testing, design-system snapshots, accessibility bug trends, and production feedback from enterprise users.
keyPoints: Test keyboard, screen reader, touch, 200%/400% zoom, narrow and wide containers, forced colors, reduced motion, localization, browser compatibility and performance budgets.

blocks.question: Why can transparent borders be useful for forced-colors support?
blocks.answer: Transparent borders can reserve space for a boundary in normal mode while allowing forced-colors mode to paint that border with a visible system color. This prevents layout shifts and gives controls an outline when backgrounds or shadows disappear.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it explains both the visual and layout reason for the technique.

title: Right-to-left layout
description: Senior/lead scenario: The application is adding Arabic and Hebrew. What CSS and UI changes are required?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
RTL support is more than flipping the page. It is about matching reading direction while preserving the meaning of data, icons, and controls.

Logical CSS properties make layouts adapt without separate left/right styles for every component.

Mixed content is where many bugs live. Arabic or Hebrew text often appears beside numbers, English product names, and IDs.
keyPoints: Use logical properties such as margin-inline, padding-block, inset-inline-start, and border-start-start-radius instead of left/right where direction should adapt.
Mirror directional icons such as arrows when meaning depends on direction, but do not mirror universal or brand icons blindly.
Test mixed-direction content, numbers, account IDs, punctuation, and input caret behavior.
Ensure charts, timelines, navigation, and animation direction follow product meaning.
Apply dir at the correct document or component boundary and verify third-party widgets.

blocks.question: The application is adding Arabic and Hebrew. What CSS and UI changes are required?
blocks.answer:
I would replace directional CSS like left, right, margin-left, and padding-right with logical properties where the layout should follow text direction. Examples are margin-inline, padding-block, and inset-inline-start.

The dir attribute should be applied at the correct boundary. Sometimes the whole document is RTL; sometimes only a component or content block is.

Directional icons need review. Back, forward, next, previous, and chevrons often mirror. Brand marks, media controls, numbers, and many status icons usually do not.

I would test mixed-direction content carefully: account IDs, phone numbers, punctuation, currencies, and form input caret behavior can all look wrong.

Charts, timelines, navigation, and animations need product decisions. Some should mirror with reading direction, while others should keep data order or time direction.

blocks.explanation: Logical properties handle direction automatically; directional icons may still need mirroring.
