blocks.content: A weak answer is to set dir=rtl on the body and assume the browser fixes the app. Hardcoded left/right CSS, icons, charts, and third-party widgets can still be wrong.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Logical properties reduce duplicate CSS, but some product areas need explicit direction rules. I would validate with native-speaking review, pseudo-RTL testing, production locale analytics, and bug reports around forms, tables, and navigation.
keyPoints: Test keyboard, screen reader, touch, 200%/400% zoom, narrow and wide containers, forced colors, reduced motion, localization, browser compatibility and performance budgets.

blocks.question: Which icons should usually not be mirrored in RTL?
blocks.answer: Icons that represent universal objects or brand identity usually should not be mirrored, such as logos, play buttons, checkmarks, warning symbols, and many file or settings icons. Icons that mean direction or navigation often should be mirrored. The decision depends on meaning, not shape.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it gives a rule based on semantic meaning instead of mirroring everything.

title: Responsive tables
description: Senior/lead scenario: A table has 30 columns and business users need comparison. What responsive strategies do you consider?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Responsive tables should respect the reason the data is in a table. If comparison matters, preserve rows, columns, and headers.

Cards are useful when each row is a record to read on its own. They are poor when users compare many records across the same fields.

A good table strategy often combines layout, personalization, and data loading instead of relying on one CSS trick.
keyPoints: Keep true tabular semantics for comparison tasks. Provide horizontal scrolling, sticky headers/key columns, column selection, and saved views.
On narrow screens, show a prioritized subset with an accessible details panel or card only if row-by-row reading is more important than cross-row comparison.
Do not use data-label pseudo-content as the only header source because assistive technology support and maintainability can be problematic.
Support keyboard navigation, focus visibility, and scroll affordances.
Combine with server paging and row virtualization for large datasets.

blocks.question: A table has 30 columns and business users need comparison. What responsive strategies do you consider?
blocks.answer:
I would keep real table semantics if users need comparison. A 30-column business table is often about scanning across rows and columns, so turning everything into cards can destroy the task.

For smaller screens, I would consider horizontal scrolling with clear affordances, sticky headers, and sticky key columns. That keeps the comparison model intact.

I would add column selection, saved views, and priority presets so users can focus the table for their job instead of seeing all 30 columns every time.

If the mobile task is row-by-row review, a summary row plus accessible details panel or card view may work. But the headers still need to be real, not only CSS-generated labels.

For large data, I would combine the responsive pattern with server paging or virtualization and keep keyboard navigation and focus visible.

blocks.explanation: Weak version to avoid: A weak answer is to stack every cell under a data-label in CSS and remove the table experience. That may be readable one row at a time but poor for business comparison.

blocks.title: Practical code / design example
blocks.explanation: Preserve table semantics and provide a deliberate small-screen strategy rather than turning every table into inaccessible cards.

blocks.title: Common weak answer
blocks.content: A weak answer is to stack every cell under a data-label in CSS and remove the table experience. That may be readable one row at a time but poor for business comparison.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Horizontal scroll preserves comparison but can be awkward on small screens. I would validate with table task completion, column customization usage, scroll depth, saved-view adoption, and production feedback from power users.
keyPoints: Test keyboard, screen reader, touch, 200%/400% zoom, narrow and wide containers, forced colors, reduced motion, localization, browser compatibility and performance budgets.

blocks.question: When would converting a table to cards damage usability?
blocks.answer: Converting a table to cards damages usability when users need to compare values across many rows or scan a column for outliers. Cards repeat labels and make vertical scrolling much longer. They can also hide the relationship between headers and values if built poorly.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it ties the layout choice to the comparison task.

title: Responsive charts
description: Senior/lead scenario: A chart becomes unreadable on small screens. How would you adapt it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A chart is a tool for answering a data question. Responsive chart work starts by deciding which insight must remain clear.

Small screens have less room for axes, legends, labels, and dense points. Reducing detail can improve accuracy if the main message stays intact.

Accessibility matters because charts are visual by default. Summaries, tables, and non-hover interactions give more users access to the data.
keyPoints: Prioritize the analytical question and reduce non-essential labels, series, and decoration rather than simply shrinking everything.
Use responsive containers and observe size changes; avoid hardcoded canvas dimensions.
Provide a textual summary and accessible data table or downloadable data for users who cannot interpret the chart.
Support touch targets, focusable data points only when useful, and non-hover access to tooltips.
For dense data, offer range selection, aggregation, or drill-down instead of plotting every point.

blocks.question: A chart becomes unreadable on small screens. How would you adapt it?
blocks.answer:
I would start with the question the chart is supposed to answer. On a small screen, we should protect that answer instead of shrinking every label and data point.

I might reduce secondary series, simplify labels, aggregate dense points, or offer drill-down. If the user needs exact values, a table or data download should be available.

The chart should size from its container, not hardcoded canvas dimensions. It should respond when the container changes, including sidebars and orientation changes.

Tooltips cannot depend only on hover. Touch and keyboard users need another way to inspect values, such as tap, focus, a persistent detail panel, or a selected data summary.

I would include a short text summary so users who cannot interpret the visual still get the main insight.

blocks.content: Simplifying a chart improves readability but may hide detail some users need. I would validate with analytics task success, tooltip usage, drill-down usage, data export clicks, and feedback from users who rely on exact values.

blocks.question: How would you make a tooltip usable on touch and keyboard devices?
blocks.answer: I would make the same information available through focus and touch, not only hover. A focused or tapped data point can open a persistent tooltip or detail panel, and Escape or another clear action can dismiss it. The trigger needs a clear name and the tooltip content should be reachable without precise mouse movement.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it describes an actual interaction model for touch and keyboard users.

title: Touch target and pointer design
description: Senior/lead scenario: Desktop icons are only 20px and become difficult to use on touch devices. How do you fix this without making the UI visually bulky?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Touch target design separates visual size from interactive size. A 20px icon can sit inside a much larger button.

Pointer type is not the same as screen size. Large screens can have touch. Small screens can have mice or trackpads. Some devices have both.

Good target design reduces mistakes without making the UI feel heavy.
keyPoints: Increase the interactive hit area using padding or a larger button box while keeping the visible icon appropriately sized.
Maintain spacing so adjacent targets are not easily activated accidentally.
Do not require hover for essential information or actions; provide focus and touch alternatives.
Use pointer and hover media features carefully as enhancement signals, not exact device detection.
Test with zoom, coarse pointers, and one-handed mobile use.

blocks.question: Desktop icons are only 20px and become difficult to use on touch devices. How do you fix this without making the UI visually bulky?
blocks.answer:
I would keep the icon visually small if that is the design goal, but make the actual button larger. Padding or a larger button box can create a comfortable hit area without making the icon look bulky.

Adjacent targets need enough spacing so users do not tap the wrong action. This matters more when actions are destructive or repeated in dense lists.

Important actions and information cannot require hover. The same content should be available on focus, tap, or always visible when it is essential.

I would use pointer and hover media features as hints. They can help tune spacing and hover behavior, but they are not exact device detection.

I would test with zoom, coarse pointers, one-handed use, and hybrid devices like touch laptops.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Larger hit areas improve accuracy, but dense enterprise screens have limited space. I would validate with tap error rates, undo/destructive-action recovery, heatmaps for missed taps, and feedback from touch and zoom users.

blocks.question: Why should device width not be used as a proxy for touch capability?
blocks.answer: Device width is a poor proxy because touch laptops, tablets with keyboards, foldables, and phones with external pointers all break that assumption. A wide viewport may still have a coarse pointer, and a narrow viewport may still support hover. Pointer and hover media features describe capability more directly, though still not perfectly.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it explains real hybrid-device cases and points to better signals.

title: CSS architecture for many teams
description: Senior/lead scenario: Twenty teams contribute styles to one application. What CSS architecture would you establish?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
CSS architecture for many teams is about reducing surprise. A good system makes the default path safe and makes risky changes obvious.

Shared values should come from tokens, not from repeated one-off values. Shared components should have public customization points, not hidden internal selectors that consumers depend on.

Global CSS should be small because global CSS has global blast radius. Component-scoped styles, layers, modules, utilities, or naming rules all try to answer the same question: who owns this rule, and where can it apply?

The final piece is governance. Linting, review rules, visual tests, and ownership keep the system from drifting back into a pile of overrides.
keyPoints: Use design tokens, component-scoped styles, an explicit cascade/layer model, and documented utility conventions.
Choose a naming approach such as BEM, component encapsulation, CSS Modules, or a controlled utility system based on build stack and team needs.
Minimize global selectors and define a small global reset/base layer only.
Expose supported component customizations through tokens, parts, classes, or inputs rather than deep selectors.
Add linting, visual regression, dead-CSS analysis, and ownership for shared styles.

blocks.question: Twenty teams contribute styles to one application. What CSS architecture would you establish?
blocks.answer:
For twenty teams, I want CSS rules that make ownership clear. The biggest risk is not syntax. It is one team changing a global selector and breaking five screens they do not own.

I would set up a small global base: reset, typography defaults, tokens, and maybe layout primitives. Everything else should live with a component, a route, or an owned package.

I would use design tokens for shared values like color, spacing, type, radius, and motion. Teams should not copy raw hex values or magic spacing into product CSS.

I would also define how the cascade works. That can mean CSS layers, CSS Modules, BEM, scoped styles, or a controlled utility system, depending on the stack. The important part is that teams know what is safe to override and what is private.

For shared components, I would expose supported hooks: tokens, props, slots, parts, or documented classes. I would not allow teams to reach into random internal DOM with deep selectors.

Finally, I would add stylelint rules, visual regression tests, dead-CSS checks, and clear ownership for shared files. Architecture only works if the review and tooling support it.

blocks.content: Strict architecture can slow down quick one-off changes, so escape hatches need to exist but be visible and reviewed. Too much utility CSS can make markup noisy; too much component isolation can make theming harder. In production, I would watch visual regression results, CSS bundle size, unused CSS, and support tickets caused by styling changes across apps.

blocks.question: What is the risk of mixing BEM, utility classes, and ad hoc global selectors without governance?
blocks.answer: Mixing all three without rules makes the cascade unpredictable. A BEM selector, a utility class, and a random global selector can all fight for the same property, and the winner may depend on import order instead of intent. Over time, teams stop trusting the system and add more specific selectors or !important to get work shipped.
blocks.explanation: It ties the naming problem to real maintenance failure: unpredictable ownership, import-order bugs, and escalating overrides.

title: BEM and naming conventions
description: Senior/lead scenario: Would you still use BEM in component-based applications?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
BEM solves a real problem: global class names need meaning and boundaries. Block, element, and modifier names make it clear which component owns a style and which variation is active.

Component systems reduce some of that pressure, but they do not remove the need for readable state and variant names. Engineers still need to understand why a style exists and what can safely change.

The danger is overusing the convention. Long names, deep nesting, and DOM-shaped selectors bring back the coupling BEM was meant to avoid.

A naming convention is good when it helps teams make consistent choices. It is bad when it becomes ceremony.
keyPoints: BEM remains useful where global CSS exists because it communicates block, element, and modifier relationships and reduces selector coupling.
Component encapsulation may reduce collision risk, but clear state and variant naming is still valuable.
Avoid excessively long names that repeat framework structure and avoid nesting selectors based on DOM depth.
Use data attributes or modifier classes for state rather than styling based on fragile positional selectors.
Select a convention that improves team consistency; BEM is a tool, not a requirement.

blocks.question: Would you still use BEM in component-based applications?
blocks.answer:
Yes, I would still use BEM in some component-based apps, but not as a rule for every project. BEM is useful when CSS is global or semi-global because the class name explains the relationship between the component, its parts, and its variants.

In a framework with strong style encapsulation or CSS Modules, collision risk is lower. Even then, clear names still matter. A class or state like button--danger or data-loading tells the next engineer what the style means.

I would avoid turning BEM into giant names that mirror the whole component tree. If the class name is longer than the idea it represents, the convention is getting in the way.

I also would not nest selectors deeply just because BEM is present. The goal is loose coupling, not a different way to describe DOM depth.

For states and variants, I prefer explicit modifier classes, data attributes, or component props that map cleanly to styles. Styling based on nth-child or fragile parent structure usually ages badly.

So my answer is: use BEM when it improves clarity and team consistency. Do not treat it as a religion.

With data attributes, it could be .button[data-variant="danger"][data-loading="true"]. The key is that danger is a visual and semantic variant, while loading is a state.

title: CSS custom properties versus Sass variables
description: Senior/lead scenario: When should you use CSS custom properties and when should you use Sass variables?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
The main difference is when the value exists. Sass variables exist while CSS is being built. CSS custom properties exist while the page is running.

That makes Sass useful for authoring and generation. It can loop through maps, call functions, and produce CSS before the browser sees it.

Custom properties are part of CSS itself. They follow inheritance and the cascade, so they are the right tool for themes, component overrides, and values that change by context.

A mature system often uses both: Sass for organizing source code, custom properties for the public runtime token layer.
keyPoints: Sass variables are resolved at build time and are useful for code generation, loops, mixins, and constants that do not change at runtime.
CSS custom properties participate in the cascade, inherit, and can change at runtime, making them ideal for themes, component tokens, and contextual values.
Custom properties can have fallback values and can be read/updated from JavaScript, but their values are strings until interpreted by a property.
Use Sass to generate a semantic custom-property system rather than duplicating theme styles.
Avoid exposing arbitrary internal variables as public tokens.

blocks.question: When should you use CSS custom properties and when should you use Sass variables?
blocks.answer:
I use Sass variables for build-time decisions and CSS custom properties for runtime decisions.

A Sass variable is gone after compilation. It is great for constants, loops, maps, mixins, and generating a family of classes or tokens during the build.

A CSS custom property still exists in the browser. It can inherit, respond to the cascade, change under a theme class, and be updated by JavaScript.

For theming, component tokens, and contextual values, I want custom properties. For example, a card can use --card-bg, and that value can change in dark mode or inside a special section without recompiling CSS.

I often use Sass to generate the custom-property system. Sass can keep token files organized, but the browser variables do the runtime work.

I would be careful about what becomes public. Not every internal value should become a token that product teams depend on forever.

blocks.answer: A Sass variable cannot respond to a runtime theme switch because it has already been replaced with a final value in the compiled CSS. The browser never sees $brand-color. To switch themes without rebuilding CSS, the value needs to be something the browser can change, like a custom property on a theme selector.

title: Sass module system
description: Senior/lead scenario: A legacy SCSS codebase uses @import and global variables everywhere. How would you modernize it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
keyPoints: Move to @use and @forward so dependencies are explicit, namespaced, and loaded once.
Create focused token, function, and mixin modules with a clear public surface.
Avoid one global file that every component imports if it emits CSS repeatedly or creates hidden coupling.
Use configuration with with only for stable build-time customization and prefer CSS custom properties for runtime themes.
Migrate incrementally and compare compiled CSS size and ordering.

blocks.question: A legacy SCSS codebase uses @import and global variables everywhere. How would you modernize it?
blocks.answer:
I would move the codebase away from @import toward @use and @forward. The goal is to make Sass dependencies explicit instead of relying on a shared global soup.

With @use, a file imports a module under a namespace. That makes it much easier to see where a variable, function, or mixin comes from.

With @forward, we can create clean public entry points. For example, a tokens module can forward only the pieces other teams should use.

I would split the old global file into focused modules: tokens, functions, mixins, and maybe component-level helpers. I would avoid importing a big file everywhere if it emits repeated CSS or creates hidden ordering rules.

For build-time configuration, I would use Sass configuration only for stable values. For runtime themes, I would move toward CSS custom properties.

I would migrate in small steps and compare compiled CSS after each batch. Sass source can look cleaner while the output gets bigger or changes order, so I would check the result, not just the source.

blocks.question: What is the practical difference between @use and @import?
blocks.answer: @import copies files into the importing stylesheet and shares members globally, which can create collisions and repeated CSS. @use loads a module once, gives it a namespace by default, and makes dependencies clearer. In practice, @use is safer for large codebases because it reduces hidden coupling.

title: Sass mixins, functions, and extends
description: Senior/lead scenario: A stylesheet uses large mixins and @extend heavily. What problems can this cause?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Sass abstractions have output costs. A mixin copies CSS where it is included. An extend changes selector relationships. A function just returns a value.

That means they should not be used interchangeably. Functions are best for calculations. Mixins are best for repeated declaration patterns. Extends need the most care because they can connect selectors that look unrelated in source files.

The healthy habit is to look at compiled CSS. If the output is huge or confusing, the abstraction is not helping, even if the Sass looks elegant.

Often, design tokens, small utilities, and clear components are easier to maintain than a large web of mixins and extends.
keyPoints: Mixins copy declarations at each include site, which can increase output size when used extensively.
@extend can create large combined selectors and surprising relationships, especially across modules.
Functions should calculate values and return results; mixins should emit declarations or rules.
Prefer design tokens and small utilities/components over abstracting every repeated line.
Inspect compiled CSS because source elegance can hide output cost.

blocks.question: A stylesheet uses large mixins and @extend heavily. What problems can this cause?
blocks.answer:
Large mixins can make the source look tidy while making the compiled CSS heavy. Every include can copy the same declarations again.

Heavy @extend use has a different risk. It can merge selectors in surprising ways, especially when modules start extending placeholders across boundaries.

I like functions for calculation. They should take inputs and return a value, like a spacing or color result.

I use mixins when I need to emit a small, clear set of declarations or rules. If a mixin turns into a mini framework, I would question it.

I am cautious with @extend. It can be useful with local placeholder selectors, but I do not want it creating large combined selectors that nobody expects.

I would inspect the compiled CSS. The source abstraction is only good if the output is understandable, maintainable, and not bloated.

title: LESS versus SCSS decision
description: Senior/lead scenario: A new project asks whether to choose LESS or SCSS. How would you decide?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
The LESS versus SCSS decision is mostly an ecosystem and maintenance decision. The language features overlap enough that team fit and tooling usually matter more.

SCSS is often attractive because of its ecosystem and module system. LESS may be practical when a product already has a LESS-based design system or third-party framework.

Native CSS should still carry runtime concerns like theming and responsive component behavior when it can. A preprocessor runs before the browser, so it should not replace browser features that solve the problem better.

The goal is a stable styling architecture, not simply a more powerful stylesheet language.
keyPoints: Both provide variables, nesting, mixins, and functions, but ecosystem, existing design-system tooling, team skill, and framework integration matter more than a feature checklist.
SCSS has a strong modern module system and broad ecosystem; LESS may fit an existing library or organization already built around it.
Avoid selecting a preprocessor merely to enable deep nesting or global variables that create architectural debt.
Prefer native CSS features such as custom properties, nesting where supported, layers, and container queries when they meet the need.
Migration and long-term maintenance cost should be part of the decision.

blocks.question: A new project asks whether to choose LESS or SCSS. How would you decide?
blocks.answer:
I would not choose LESS or SCSS from a feature checklist alone. Both can handle variables, nesting, mixins, and functions.

The better question is what the project already depends on. If the design system, build tools, and team experience are already centered on SCSS, SCSS is usually the safer choice.

SCSS also has a strong modern module system, which matters in larger codebases. Namespaced modules and controlled public APIs help keep styles maintainable.

LESS can still be the right choice if the organization or a major UI library already uses it heavily. Avoiding a mismatch can be more valuable than picking the more popular tool.

I would also ask whether we need a preprocessor at all for a given problem. Native CSS now covers many needs with custom properties, layers, nesting, and container queries.

The bad reason to choose either tool is to enable deep nesting and global variables everywhere. That just creates CSS debt with a nicer syntax.

title: Nesting depth
description: Senior/lead scenario: A SCSS file has selectors nested six levels deep. Why is this risky?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Nesting is attractive because it mirrors the HTML. The problem is that CSS selectors are not just organization; they are contracts with the DOM.

When nesting gets deep, the selector starts saying, this style only works when the markup has this exact shape. That makes refactors risky and overrides harder.

The better approach is to style named component parts and states. The selector should describe meaning, not every wrapper in the markup.

A practical nesting limit keeps Sass readable while stopping accidental specificity growth.
keyPoints: Deep nesting creates highly specific selectors coupled to DOM structure and makes reuse and overrides difficult.
Compiled selectors can become large and slow to reason about, even if the source looks organized.
Limit nesting primarily to states, pseudo-elements, and direct component relationships.
Extract subcomponents or use explicit class names rather than mirroring every DOM level.
Use stylelint rules to enforce a practical nesting limit.

blocks.question: A SCSS file has selectors nested six levels deep. Why is this risky?
blocks.answer:
Six levels of SCSS nesting is a warning sign. The source may look organized, but the compiled selector is probably tied tightly to the current DOM.

That makes the component hard to reuse. If someone wraps a label, changes a div, or moves an icon, the style can break for reasons that are not obvious.

Deep nesting also raises specificity. Then later changes need even more specific selectors, and the file starts a cascade arms race.

I would flatten the selectors around meaningful classes. If a nested piece is important enough to style, it probably deserves a class or a subcomponent.

Some nesting is fine. States, pseudo-classes, pseudo-elements, and small direct relationships can be readable.

I would add a stylelint nesting-depth rule so the team catches this before it becomes a pattern.

blocks.question: What kinds of nesting are generally safe and readable?
blocks.answer: Safe nesting is usually close to the component class: hover, focus, disabled states, pseudo-elements, and direct child parts when the relationship is stable. For example, .button { &:hover {} &::before {} } is easy to follow. Mirroring six DOM wrappers is not.

title: Removing unused CSS
description: Senior/lead scenario: The production CSS bundle is 2 MB and contains years of legacy rules. How would you reduce it safely?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Unused CSS is risky to remove because CSS usage is not always visible from static HTML. Classes may come from feature flags, CMS content, runtime state, or user permissions.

The safe approach combines runtime coverage, static analysis, ownership knowledge, and tests. No single tool has the full truth.

Splitting CSS by route or component reduces the problem at the source. Instead of one global pile, each part of the app pays for the styles it needs.

The cleanup should be incremental. Small deletes with clear rollback paths are safer than one giant purge.
keyPoints: Measure coverage across representative routes and states, but do not delete solely from one browser session because dynamic classes may be missed.
Split styles by route/component, remove unused framework modules/themes, and migrate global rules into owned components.
Use static analysis with explicit safelists for dynamic class names and validate with visual regression and end-to-end tests.
Track CSS size budgets and prevent new global additions without review.
Delete in small batches with rollback and production monitoring.

blocks.question: The production CSS bundle is 2 MB and contains years of legacy rules. How would you reduce it safely?
blocks.answer:
I would start by measuring, not deleting. A single coverage run can tell us some useful things, but it will miss routes, permissions, experiments, dynamic states, and classes built at runtime.

I would gather coverage across representative pages and user flows. That includes logged-in states, error states, modals, admin screens, and localized content.

Then I would split CSS by route or component where the build allows it. A 2 MB global bundle often means every page is paying for styles it never uses.

I would remove unused framework modules, old themes, and orphaned global rules in small batches. For dynamic class names, I would use explicit safelists instead of trusting purge tools blindly.

Visual regression and end-to-end tests are important here because CSS deletion bugs can be subtle. The page may still load but a rare state may look broken.

After cleanup, I would add size budgets and review rules so the bundle does not slowly grow back.

title: Cross-browser compatibility
description: Senior/lead scenario: A component works in the latest Chrome but fails in an enterprise-managed browser. What process do you follow?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Cross-browser work starts with a support contract. Without that, teams waste time fixing browsers nobody uses or breaking users the business promised to support.

Once the target is clear, debug the capability. Modern browser issues are often about one feature, one syntax form, or one engine bug rather than the whole browser.

Feature detection is usually more reliable than browser detection because browsers change. If the capability exists, use it. If it does not, provide a fallback or load a focused polyfill.

The process should end in tests and documentation so the same issue does not come back every release.
keyPoints: Start with the supported browser matrix based on users and contracts, not assumptions.
Check feature support, syntax, vendor bugs, polyfill/transpilation targets, and progressive enhancement options.
Use feature queries and capability detection rather than browser sniffing where possible.
Automate representative browser tests and keep a small manual device lab for interaction/accessibility edge cases.
Document intentional degradation and remove old workarounds when support policy changes.

blocks.question: A component works in the latest Chrome but fails in an enterprise-managed browser. What process do you follow?
blocks.answer:
I would first check the supported browser policy. The answer depends on our users, contracts, and enterprise requirements, not just what works on my machine.

Then I would isolate what is failing. It could be unsupported syntax, a missing API, a prefix issue, a browser bug, a transpilation target, or a polyfill gap.

If the feature is optional, I would use progressive enhancement. The newer browser gets the nicer behavior, and the older supported browser still gets a usable experience.

For CSS, I would use @supports where it helps. For JavaScript, I would use capability detection rather than guessing from the browser name when possible.

I would add automated coverage for the supported browsers on important flows. Some interaction and accessibility issues still need manual checks on real devices or managed browser builds.

I would also document any intentional fallback. Old workarounds should have an owner so they can be removed when support changes.

blocks.question: When is user-agent detection justified?
blocks.answer: User-agent detection is justified when the problem is a known browser or engine bug that cannot be detected through a feature test. Even then, I would keep the check narrow, documented, and temporary. Capability detection should still be the default.

title: Progressive enhancement
description: Senior/lead scenario: A critical form depends on a new browser feature. How would you preserve functionality for unsupported browsers?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Progressive enhancement means the basic experience is real, not fake. The app starts from something that works, then adds richer behavior when the browser can support it.

This is especially important for critical workflows like forms, payments, authentication, and account recovery. Those flows should not depend on a fragile advanced layer.

Feature detection is the switch. If the browser supports the capability, enhance. If not, keep the baseline path.

A good enhanced experience shares the same data rules and error language as the fallback, so users are not punished for their browser.
keyPoints: Start with semantic HTML and a basic server/API workflow that completes the core task.
Detect the feature and enhance the interaction where available rather than serving a broken advanced experience.
Use @supports for CSS capabilities and runtime feature detection for JavaScript APIs.
Keep error and validation behavior consistent across enhanced and fallback paths.
Measure the affected user population before adding large polyfills.

blocks.question: A critical form depends on a new browser feature. How would you preserve functionality for unsupported browsers?
blocks.answer:
For a critical form, the core task must work without the new feature. A user should still be able to enter data, submit it, see errors, and complete the workflow.

I would start with semantic HTML and a server or API path that handles the real submission. That gives us a reliable baseline.

Then I would detect the new feature and enhance the experience only when it is available. The enhanced path might be faster, smoother, or more interactive, but it should not be the only working path.

For CSS, @supports can gate newer layout or styling behavior. For JavaScript APIs, I would use runtime feature checks before using the API.

Validation and error messages need to feel consistent across both paths. A fallback that submits but gives confusing errors is still a bad experience.

Before adding a large polyfill, I would measure how many supported users need it and whether the feature is worth the weight.

blocks.question: How is progressive enhancement different from graceful degradation?
blocks.answer: Progressive enhancement starts with a working baseline and adds advanced features when possible. Graceful degradation often starts with the advanced experience and then tries to make it fail acceptably in weaker environments. In practice, progressive enhancement is safer for critical flows because the fallback is designed from the start.

title: Printing and PDF-friendly CSS
description: Senior/lead scenario: A web report must print cleanly and be exported to PDF. What CSS and layout concerns do you address?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Print is a different medium. The browser has to break one scrolling page into physical pages, and that changes layout rules.

Good print CSS decides what content belongs in the document and what screen-only UI should disappear. It also controls typography, contrast, page breaks, and table behavior.

PDF export adds another layer. Some PDFs are just convenience exports, while others are legal or financial records that need deterministic pagination, fonts, totals, and headers.

The more regulated the document, the less I would trust a screenshot-style export of the live UI.
keyPoints: Create dedicated print styles that remove interactive chrome, expand necessary content, and use print-appropriate typography and contrast.
Control page breaks with break-before/after/inside where supported and prevent important rows/headings from being orphaned.
Repeat table headers, avoid fixed-position overlays, and ensure backgrounds are not the only carrier of meaning.
Use physical units only where print requirements justify them and test multiple browsers/renderers.
For high-volume regulated documents, prefer a server-side document generation pipeline over screenshotting complex UI.

blocks.question: A web report must print cleanly and be exported to PDF. What CSS and layout concerns do you address?
blocks.answer:
A screen layout does not automatically make a good printed report. Printing has pages, margins, page breaks, missing hover states, and different color behavior.

I would create dedicated print styles. They should remove navigation and interactive chrome, expand the content that matters, and use type and contrast that work on paper.

I would handle page breaks deliberately. Headings should not be left alone at the bottom of a page, important table rows should not split badly, and tables should repeat headers when possible.

I would avoid relying on background colors or shadows to carry meaning because printing may drop them. Text, borders, and clear labels are safer.

Fixed overlays and sticky UI often print poorly, so I would turn those off or restyle them for print.

For regulated, high-volume PDFs, I would consider server-side document generation. A browser screenshot of a complex UI is usually not reliable enough.

blocks.answer: A perfect screen layout can fail in print because the screen scrolls continuously while paper is split into pages. Fixed headers, sticky panels, hidden overflow, background colors, and wide tables can all break once pagination starts. Print needs its own rules for what to show and where page breaks are allowed.

title: Design tokens across platforms
description: Senior/lead scenario: Design wants one token source for web, mobile, and documents. How would you structure it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Cross-platform tokens work best when they describe decisions, not just values. The token name should explain the role the value plays in the UI.

Primitive tokens are raw ingredients. Semantic tokens say how those ingredients are used. Component tokens apply them to a specific component contract.

Different platforms may need different output formats and sometimes different values. A shadow, font, or color may need adjustment to feel correct and accessible on each platform.

Treating tokens as a versioned API helps teams change the system without breaking every consumer at once.
keyPoints: Define platform-neutral semantic tokens with metadata, references, and modes, then transform them into CSS variables, Sass maps, mobile resources, and documentation.
Separate primitive palette/spacing values from semantic roles and component-specific tokens.
Version tokens and treat destructive renames as API changes with migration guidance.
Validate references, contrast, units, and unsupported platform concepts in CI.
Do not force every platform to use identical rendered values when platform conventions differ.

blocks.question: Design wants one token source for web, mobile, and documents. How would you structure it?
blocks.answer:
I would create one source of truth for token meaning, not force every platform to render identical pixels.

The token system should separate primitive values from semantic roles. For example, blue-600 is a primitive, but action-background or text-danger is semantic.

Component tokens are another layer. A button may have button-primary-bg that points to a semantic token, and that can transform differently for web, iOS, Android, and documents.

The source should include metadata, modes, references, descriptions, and platform constraints. Then a build step can transform it into CSS variables, Sass maps, mobile resources, and docs.

I would version tokens like an API. Removing or renaming a token can break products, so those changes need migration notes.

CI should validate references, units, contrast, and unsupported platform concepts before tokens ship.

Too many component tokens can become hard to manage; too few force unsafe overrides. blocks.question: What is the difference between primitive, semantic, and component tokens?
blocks.answer: Primitive tokens are raw values like blue-600, space-4, or font-size-16. Semantic tokens describe purpose, like text-muted, surface-raised, or border-danger. Component tokens are specific to a component, like button-primary-background or tab-active-border.

title: Visual regression testing
description: Senior/lead scenario: A design-system change breaks spacing in several products. How would visual regression testing help?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Visual regression testing is a safety net for appearance. It compares the current UI to a known good version and highlights differences.

It works best with deterministic examples. If the screenshot changes for random reasons, the team stops trusting the test.

Thresholds are a balance. Too strict creates noise. Too loose hides real regressions. The right setting depends on the component and risk.

Visual tests are strongest in design systems because shared components have many downstream consumers. One baseline review can protect many products.
keyPoints: Capture stable component stories and critical page states at controlled viewport, font, data, and browser conditions.
Compare screenshots with reviewed baselines and use thresholds carefully so meaningful small changes are not ignored.
Mask nondeterministic areas such as timestamps or animation and freeze data/time where possible.
Visual tests complement, not replace, semantic accessibility and interaction tests.
Require human review for intended changes and store baseline ownership with the component team.

blocks.question: A design-system change breaks spacing in several products. How would visual regression testing help?
blocks.answer:
Visual regression testing would catch spacing changes by comparing known UI states against reviewed baselines. It is especially useful for design-system changes because one small token or component edit can affect many products.

I would capture stable component stories and critical page states. The test data, viewport, fonts, browser, and time should be controlled as much as possible.

I would keep thresholds tight enough to catch real spacing changes. If the threshold is too loose, the test gives a false sense of safety.

At the same time, I would mask things that are naturally unstable, like timestamps, charts with random data, loading shimmer, or animations.

A human still needs to approve intended baseline changes. The test should show what changed; it should not decide whether the design is correct.

I would pair visual tests with interaction and accessibility tests. Screenshots can catch pixels, but they do not prove the component works.

blocks.question: Why can pixel-perfect screenshot tests become noisy?
blocks.answer: Pixel-perfect tests become noisy when tiny differences do not matter to users but still fail the build. Font rendering, anti-aliasing, animation timing, dynamic data, and browser differences can all move pixels. Good visual testing controls those inputs and masks areas that are not part of the assertion.

title: CSS debugging with DevTools
description: Senior/lead scenario: A component style is unexpectedly overridden. Describe your debugging sequence.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
CSS debugging is about following the cascade before changing code. DevTools can tell you which rules matched, which value won, and whether the value came from inheritance.

Not every visual bug is a cascade bug. Layout tools can reveal flex shrinking, grid track sizing, overflow clipping, and stacking context issues.

State also matters. A component may look wrong because a media query, container query, or pseudo-class is active.

A good debugging sequence narrows the problem to one rule or one layout relationship, then fixes the owner instead of adding another override.
keyPoints: Inspect the element, computed styles, matched rules, inherited values, cascade layer, specificity, source order, and !important origin.
Check layout panels for grid/flex sizing, box model, overflow, and containing/stacking contexts.
Toggle declarations and classes to isolate the minimal cause rather than editing random selectors.
Inspect media/container query matches and pseudo-class state.
Fix the owning rule or component API, then add a regression test if the bug is likely to recur.

blocks.question: A component style is unexpectedly overridden. Describe your debugging sequence.
blocks.answer:
I would inspect the element first, not guess at selectors. The matched rules and computed styles usually show which declaration is winning and why.

I would check specificity, source order, cascade layer, inheritance, and whether !important is involved. If a value is crossed out, DevTools can usually show the rule that beat it.

Then I would look at layout context. Grid, flex, box model, overflow, stacking contexts, and containing blocks can make a style look ignored when the real issue is layout.

I would also check active media queries, container queries, and pseudo-states like hover, focus, disabled, or selected. A rule may only apply in a state I am not currently simulating.

I like toggling classes and declarations to find the smallest cause. Randomly adding a stronger selector often hides the real problem.

Once I know the cause, I would fix the owning rule or expose a proper component API. If the bug is likely to come back, I would add a visual or interaction test.

title: Responsive navigation
description: Senior/lead scenario: A desktop mega-menu must work on mobile and keyboard. How would you design it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Responsive navigation is not only a layout problem. It is an interaction problem.

A desktop mega-menu often depends on hover and wide space. Mobile and keyboard users need explicit controls and clear state instead.

The semantics should remain stable: links go somewhere, buttons change the current view. That keeps behavior easier to understand and test.

When the pattern changes to a drawer or accordion, focus and close behavior must match whether it is modal or simply expanded content.
keyPoints: Keep navigation semantics and link destinations consistent, but adapt the interaction pattern rather than squeezing the desktop hover menu.
Use explicit buttons to expand submenus, expose expanded state, and support Escape and predictable focus movement.
Do not rely on hover; ensure touch and keyboard can access every destination.
When using a mobile drawer, trap focus only if it is modal and return focus to the menu button on close.
Test long labels, RTL, zoom, and deep menu levels; simplify information architecture if nesting is excessive.

blocks.question: A desktop mega-menu must work on mobile and keyboard. How would you design it?
blocks.answer:
I would not try to squeeze the desktop mega-menu into a phone layout. The destinations can stay the same, but the interaction should fit the input method and space.

Top-level navigation should use real links for navigation and buttons for expanding groups. If a submenu opens, the control needs an expanded state that assistive tech can understand.

Hover cannot be the only way to use the menu. Touch and keyboard users need a direct way to open, move through, and close navigation.

On mobile, a drawer or accordion pattern may work better than a mega-menu. If the drawer is modal, focus should stay inside while it is open and return to the menu button when it closes.

Escape should close open menus where that behavior makes sense. Focus movement should be predictable and visible.

I would also challenge excessive nesting. If the menu needs five levels on mobile, the information architecture may need work, not just CSS.

blocks.question: Should arrow keys be required in a website navigation menu?
blocks.answer: Arrow keys are not always required for normal website navigation. If it is built as a simple list of links with buttons that expand sections, Tab and Shift+Tab may be enough. Arrow-key behavior becomes more relevant when you implement a true application-style menu pattern, and then you need to follow that pattern fully.

title: CSS for localization expansion
description: Senior/lead scenario: German and Finnish translations are much longer than English and break buttons and tabs. How do you prepare the UI?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Localization expansion means the UI must be content-driven. Text length changes by language, and some scripts have different spacing, line-height, and reading patterns.

Rigid dimensions usually fail. Flexible containers, wrapping, min and max widths, and well-designed overflow patterns make the UI more resilient.

Pseudo-localization is valuable because it catches layout bugs while the feature is still cheap to change.

The design system should include localized examples so teams do not build components that only fit English.
keyPoints: Avoid fixed widths and fixed heights for text containers. Use flexible sizing, wrapping, min/max constraints, and content-driven layout.
Do not truncate essential actions without an accessible way to read the full label.
Pseudo-localize early with expanded strings and accented characters to expose assumptions before translation.
Allow buttons and tabs to grow or move into overflow patterns while preserving touch targets.
Coordinate concise UX copy with translators instead of coding English-specific exceptions.

blocks.question: German and Finnish translations are much longer than English and break buttons and tabs. How do you prepare the UI?
blocks.answer:
I would design the layout to expect longer text from the start. English is often one of the shortest versions of the UI.

Fixed button widths and fixed text heights are the first things I would remove. Labels need room to wrap or containers need a clear overflow pattern.

Essential action text should not be silently truncated. If truncation is unavoidable in a dense area, the full label needs to be available in an accessible way.

Tabs and buttons may need to grow, wrap, scroll, or move into an overflow menu. The choice depends on whether users need to compare items or just access actions.

I would add pseudo-localization early. Expanded strings and accented characters expose assumptions before real translations arrive.

I would also work with content design and translators. Sometimes the right fix is better source copy, not a CSS exception for one language.

blocks.question: How would you design tabs when labels cannot fit in one row?
blocks.answer: If tab labels cannot fit in one row, I would first see whether wrapping is readable and still easy to scan. If there are many tabs, a horizontal scroll with clear affordance or an overflow menu may be better. I would avoid cutting off labels without a way to read the full text.

title: Accessible notifications and toasts
description: Senior/lead scenario: A toast disappears after three seconds and contains an important failure message. What is wrong?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Notifications should match the importance of the message. Temporary toasts are fine for low-risk feedback, but they are weak for critical or actionable information.

Accessibility also depends on announcement behavior. Live regions can inform users without stealing focus, but overusing assertive announcements makes the app noisy.

Focus should move only when the user needs to act in a new place. Non-actionable messages usually should be announced, not focused.

If a message affects task completion, it should remain available until the user can understand and address it.
keyPoints: Critical or actionable information should remain available in the page or an error region; a transient toast alone is easy to miss.
Use appropriate live-region politeness and avoid interrupting the user with every minor success.
Do not move focus to non-actionable toasts. If actions exist, provide sufficient time and keyboard access.
Pause or extend timing when users hover/focus only when that pattern remains understandable.
Keep a notification history for important events where the product requires it.

blocks.question: A toast disappears after three seconds and contains an important failure message. What is wrong?
blocks.answer:
The problem is that an important failure message disappears too quickly. A toast is easy to miss, especially for screen-reader users, keyboard users, or anyone looking away.

For critical errors, I would keep the message available in the page near the affected area or in a persistent error region. A toast can be a secondary signal, not the only place the error exists.

The live region should match the urgency. Minor success messages should not interrupt the user, but serious failures may need stronger announcement.

I would not move focus to a plain toast that has no action. That can be disorienting. If the toast has actions, those actions need keyboard access and enough time to use them.

Auto-dismiss timing should be used carefully. Hover or focus pause can help, but the pattern must still be understandable.

For products where events matter, I would keep a notification history so users can recover missed messages.

blocks.question: When should aria-live="assertive" be used?
blocks.answer: aria-live="assertive" should be reserved for urgent messages that need immediate attention, such as a failed save that blocks the current task or a session timeout warning. It interrupts screen-reader output, so I would not use it for routine success toasts or low-priority updates. Most notifications should use polite or be shown persistently without interruption.

title: Icon-only controls
description: Senior/lead scenario: A toolbar uses only icons and several are ambiguous. How would you improve it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Icon-only controls save space but increase ambiguity. The UI has to provide meaning in a way that works visually and programmatically.

An accessible name is what assistive technology uses to identify the control. A tooltip is a visual or interaction aid. They may contain the same words, but they are not the same mechanism.

Important actions benefit from visible labels because all users can understand them faster. Tooltips are best as support, not as the only explanation.

The rest of the button behavior still matters: target size, focus, state, and disabled handling.
keyPoints: Provide an accessible name through visible text, aria-label, or associated tooltip, and ensure the name describes the action.
Use familiar icons but do not assume every user understands them; important or uncommon actions should include visible labels where space permits.
Tooltips must work with keyboard and touch and should not contain essential information available nowhere else.
Maintain target size, focus style, pressed/expanded state, and disabled explanation.
Decorative icons should be hidden from assistive technology to avoid duplicate announcements.

blocks.question: A toolbar uses only icons and several are ambiguous. How would you improve it?
blocks.answer:
I would first make sure every icon-only control has a clear accessible name. The name should describe the action, like Delete invoice, not just Trash icon.

If the action is important or the icon is ambiguous, I would add visible text where space allows. Icons are not a universal language.

Tooltips can help, but they are not a replacement for a name. They must work for keyboard and touch, and the user should not need hover to understand a critical action.

The control should still be a real button or link, depending on what it does. It needs visible focus, enough hit area, and correct pressed, expanded, or disabled state.

Decorative icons inside labeled controls should be hidden from assistive technology so users do not hear duplicate or confusing names.

For disabled icon buttons, I would explain why the action is unavailable when that matters, not leave users guessing.

blocks.question: What is the difference between an icon’s accessible name and its visible tooltip?
blocks.answer: The accessible name is the programmatic label that screen readers and voice control use for the control. title: HTML sanitization and UI rendering
description: Senior/lead scenario: The UI needs to show user-generated comments with limited formatting. What frontend and backend controls are needed?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Rendering user content is a trust boundary. The safest default is to treat content as text and encode it.

If formatting is needed, define a small allowed language instead of accepting full HTML. The renderer should know exactly which tags, attributes, and URL schemes are permitted.

Sanitization should happen before content is stored or shared, and again before risky rendering if the frontend accepts HTML-like input. Different layers catch different mistakes.

Security controls should be layered: allowlisted rendering, sanitizer updates, CSP, Trusted Types, safe links, and malicious payload tests.
keyPoints: Prefer a structured rich-text format or Markdown subset with an allowlisted renderer over arbitrary HTML.
Sanitize on the backend and at the rendering boundary according to the trust model, and encode plain text output by default.
Block dangerous URLs, event attributes, scripts, risky SVG/style content, and unsafe embeds.
Use CSP and Trusted Types as defense in depth and keep sanitizer dependencies updated.
Test malicious payloads and ensure links use safe target/rel behavior.

blocks.question: The UI needs to show user-generated comments with limited formatting. What frontend and backend controls are needed?
blocks.answer:
I would avoid rendering arbitrary user HTML. For comments with limited formatting, I would prefer a structured rich-text format or a small Markdown subset with an allowlisted renderer.

Plain text should be encoded by default. Formatting should be allowed only for known safe elements and attributes.

Sanitization belongs on the backend and at the rendering boundary, based on the trust model. The backend protects stored and shared content; the frontend protects the actual DOM insertion point.

The allowlist needs to block more than script tags. Dangerous URLs, event handlers, unsafe SVG, style content, iframes, and embeds can all create XSS paths.

I would add CSP and Trusted Types where supported as defense in depth. They do not replace sanitization, but they reduce damage if a path is missed.

I would test with known malicious payloads and keep sanitizer dependencies updated. Links also need safe target and rel behavior.

blocks.question: Why is stripping only script tags not sufficient to prevent XSS?
blocks.answer: Stripping only script tags is not enough because XSS can come from event attributes, javascript: URLs, unsafe SVG, CSS injection, iframes, and malformed markup that the browser repairs in dangerous ways. An attacker does not need a literal script tag to run code. The safer approach is an allowlist of known-safe elements, attributes, and URL schemes.
blocks.explanation: It gives concrete non-script attack paths and points back to allowlisting as the stronger model.

title: Responsive layout for 200% and 400% zoom
description: Senior/lead scenario: The desktop page passes at normal size but becomes unusable at 400% zoom. How would you design for reflow?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Zoom support is about reflow. Users who zoom are asking for larger content, not a broken desktop layout inside a small window.

Flexible layouts, wrapping text, and growing containers let content remain readable without clipping. Fixed dimensions are the usual source of failure.

Sticky UI can help at normal size and hurt at high zoom. It needs limits so it does not cover the content users came to read.

The rule of thumb is that normal documents and forms should work in one direction. Complex canvases and large tables may need special handling.
keyPoints: Use flexible layouts that reflow into one dimension rather than requiring two-direction scrolling for ordinary content.
Avoid fixed pixel heights and widths that clip text or controls. Let text wrap and containers grow.
Keep sticky/fixed content from consuming most of the viewport and ensure controls remain reachable.
Test browser zoom, text-only zoom where relevant, and large default font settings.
Treat zoom testing as part of responsive design, not a separate accessibility afterthought.

blocks.question: The desktop page passes at normal size but becomes unusable at 400% zoom. How would you design for reflow?
blocks.answer:
I would treat 400% zoom as part of responsive design. At that size, the layout is effectively a narrow viewport, and the page needs to reflow.

Ordinary content should not require scrolling both horizontally and vertically. A single-column flow is usually the safest pattern.

I would remove fixed pixel heights and widths that clip text. Text should wrap, containers should grow, and controls should remain reachable.

Sticky and fixed headers need special attention. At high zoom, they can consume most of the screen and trap the user in a tiny content area.

I would test browser zoom, text-only zoom where relevant, and larger default font settings. These catch different failures.

Some content, like large data grids or maps, may need two-dimensional scrolling. But that should be an exception tied to the content type, not the default page layout.

blocks.question: Which content types may legitimately require two-dimensional scrolling?
blocks.answer: Large data tables, maps, diagrams, spreadsheets, timelines, and design canvases may legitimately need two-dimensional scrolling. The key is that the content itself is spatial or comparative. A normal article, form, or settings page should not require it.
blocks.explanation: It separates content that is inherently two-dimensional from layouts that are just failing to reflow.

title: Design handoff and implementation quality
description: Senior/lead scenario: Design provides a desktop Figma screen but no responsive behavior, states, or accessibility details. What does a frontend lead do?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Design handoff is not just receiving a picture. It is turning a visual idea into a working product across states, devices, inputs, and user needs.

Missing states are normal, but they cannot stay implicit. Loading, empty, error, disabled, permission, and responsive behavior all need decisions.

A frontend lead helps by making unknowns visible and proposing sensible defaults. That keeps momentum without hiding product decisions in code.

Good implementation also feeds the design system. Reusable states, tokens, and patterns reduce future handoff gaps.
keyPoints: Do not guess silently. Run a design-engineering review covering breakpoints, content priority, focus, keyboard, loading, empty, error, validation, permissions, localization, and motion.
Translate visual values into reusable tokens and component states rather than copying isolated pixel values.
Prototype difficult interactions early and review them with design and product on real devices.
Document decisions and feed reusable patterns back into the design system.
Keep delivery moving by proposing concrete defaults and escalating only decisions with real product impact.

blocks.question: Design provides a desktop Figma screen but no responsive behavior, states, or accessibility details. What does a frontend lead do?
blocks.answer:
I would not silently guess everything missing from the desktop Figma screen. As the frontend lead, I would turn the handoff into a design-engineering review.

I would ask about responsive behavior, content priority, loading, empty states, errors, validation, permissions, focus, keyboard use, localization, and motion. Those are usually where production bugs appear.

I would translate visual values into tokens and component states instead of copying isolated pixels. If a spacing or color is part of the system, it should come from the system.

For risky interactions, I would prototype early and review on real screen sizes and input types. It is cheaper to find a bad pattern before the feature is built fully.

I would document the decisions and feed reusable patterns back into the design system. The next team should not have to rediscover the same behavior.

To keep delivery moving, I would propose concrete defaults and only escalate decisions that affect product meaning, risk, or user success.

blocks.question: Which missing design states most often create production defects?
blocks.answer: The missing states that most often create defects are loading, empty, error, disabled, validation, permission-denied, and partial-data states. Responsive behavior and focus states are close behind. These states often get less visual attention but happen constantly in real products.

title: Building an accessible component library
description: Senior/lead scenario: You own a UI library used by 30 applications. What quality gates would you require?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
An accessible component library is a shared contract. It gives product teams safe building blocks and clear rules for composition.

Documentation must cover behavior, not just props. Engineers need to know focus rules, keyboard shortcuts, labeling requirements, and content limits.

Automated tests catch many regressions, but they cannot prove every accessibility behavior. Complex interactions still need human review with keyboard and assistive tech.

The library also needs change management: stable APIs, deprecations, migration guides, and tracking of defects across consumers.
keyPoints: Document semantics, keyboard interactions, focus behavior, content guidance, responsive behavior, and supported variants for every component.
Run unit/interaction tests, automated accessibility checks, manual screen-reader/keyboard reviews for complex components, and visual regression.
Expose stable theming and composition APIs without deep selectors. Provide migration paths and deprecation notices.
Test high contrast, dark mode, RTL, localization expansion, reduced motion, zoom, and browser support.
Provide usage lint rules or schematics for common mistakes and track accessibility defects across consumers.

blocks.question: You own a UI library used by 30 applications. What quality gates would you require?
blocks.answer:
For a library used by 30 apps, I would require quality gates before components ship. A bug in the library becomes a bug everywhere.

Each component needs documentation for semantics, keyboard behavior, focus behavior, responsive behavior, content guidance, and supported variants. Consumers should not have to reverse-engineer how to use it safely.

I would test with unit tests, interaction tests, automated accessibility checks, and visual regression. For complex widgets, I would also require manual keyboard and screen-reader review.

Theming and composition APIs need to be stable. Consumers should not style internal DOM with deep selectors because that makes library changes dangerous.

I would include high contrast, dark mode, RTL, localization expansion, reduced motion, zoom, and browser support in acceptance checks.

Finally, I would provide lint rules, examples, or schematics for common misuse. A good library prevents mistakes, not just documents the ideal path.

blocks.question: Which components require the most manual accessibility testing?
blocks.answer: Dialogs, menus, comboboxes, date pickers, data grids, tree views, drag-and-drop, and rich text editors need the most manual accessibility testing. They have complex focus rules, keyboard expectations, and screen-reader announcements. Automated checks can help, but they will not fully verify the interaction model.
blocks.explanation: It identifies high-risk components and explains why automation alone is not enough.

title: Performance budget for UI assets
description: Senior/lead scenario: Marketing adds multiple fonts, icon packs, animations, and third-party scripts. How do you manage the performance impact?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A performance budget turns vague concerns into clear limits. It helps teams decide whether an asset is worth its cost.

UI assets affect more than download size. Fonts can delay text, scripts can block interaction, images affect LCP, and late-loading content can cause CLS.

The best optimization is often choosing a smaller asset or loading it later. Subsetting, lazy loading, consent-based loading, and route-based loading keep the critical path cleaner.

Budgets need ownership. Without review and exceptions, every small addition feels harmless until the page is slow.
keyPoints: Set budgets for JavaScript, CSS, fonts, images, third-party requests, LCP, CLS, and interaction latency tied to target devices/networks.
Require evidence for new assets and prefer subsetted fonts, SVG symbols, optimized images, and lazy-loaded optional experiences.
Load third parties after consent and after the critical task where possible, with timeouts and failure isolation.
Track real-user performance by release and route, and define an exception process with owner and expiry.
Performance is a product requirement and should be reviewed alongside visual quality.

blocks.question: Marketing adds multiple fonts, icon packs, animations, and third-party scripts. How do you manage the performance impact?
blocks.answer:
I would make performance a product constraint, not a late cleanup task. Fonts, icon packs, animations, and third-party scripts all need a budget.

The budget should cover JavaScript, CSS, fonts, images, third-party requests, LCP, CLS, and interaction latency. It should be tied to real target devices and networks, not a fast developer laptop.

For new assets, I would ask for evidence. Can we subset the font? Use one variable font? Replace an icon pack with selected SVGs? Lazy-load an animation?

Third-party scripts need extra scrutiny. They should load after consent and after the critical user task where possible, with timeouts and failure isolation.

I would create an exception process. If marketing needs something heavy, it should have an owner, a reason, and an expiry or review date.

Then I would track real-user performance by route and release. Lab tests are useful, but real users show the actual cost.

title: Responsive email-like or printable statements
description: Senior/lead scenario: A statement layout must work on screen, print, and downloadable PDF. Should one CSS layout handle all three?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Statements look similar across screen, print, and PDF, but the constraints are different. A shared source of data does not require one shared layout.

The screen is interactive and fluid. Print is paginated. PDF may be a formal record with strict output requirements.

Sharing tokens, formatting rules, and semantic data keeps the experiences consistent. Separate templates can still be the right choice when layout rules differ enough.

For financial or regulated statements, correctness matters as much as appearance. Totals, dates, locales, and page numbering need verification.
keyPoints: Share semantic data and design tokens, but allow separate presentation templates when output constraints differ significantly.
Screen needs responsive interaction; print needs page fragmentation; regulated PDF may require deterministic fonts, headers, footers, and pagination.
Avoid screenshot-based export for critical documents because text selection, accessibility, and pagination suffer.
Validate numbers, locale, timezone, and page totals against backend data.
Use visual regression and sample document approval across formats.

blocks.question: A statement layout must work on screen, print, and downloadable PDF. Should one CSS layout handle all three?
blocks.answer:
I would not assume one CSS layout should handle screen, print, and PDF. The data and tokens can be shared, but the presentation may need separate templates.

Screen layouts need responsive interaction. Users may filter, expand, copy, search, or navigate through the statement.

Print layouts need page rules. They need good page breaks, readable type, repeated headers, and content that makes sense without interactive controls.

PDFs, especially regulated ones, may need deterministic fonts, headers, footers, page totals, pagination, and archived output that matches approvals.

I would avoid screenshot-based export for important documents. It hurts text selection, accessibility, search, file size, and pagination.

I would validate numbers, locale, time zone, totals, and sample documents against backend data across all formats.

blocks.question: What factors justify a server-side PDF template instead of browser print CSS?
blocks.answer: A server-side PDF template is justified when the document is regulated, high volume, archived, or must have exact pagination, headers, footers, fonts, and totals. It is also stronger when PDFs are generated in batch or sent without a browser session. Browser print CSS is fine for simpler user-initiated exports, but it is less deterministic.
blocks.explanation: It ties the server-side choice to determinism, compliance, scale, and browser independence.

title: Senior UI architecture judgment
description: Senior/lead scenario: A design team proposes a completely custom control for every native form element. How do you evaluate it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Senior UI judgment means seeing the full cost of a design choice. A custom control may look simple in a mockup but replace a large amount of platform behavior.

Native controls already handle many hard cases: focus, input methods, accessibility APIs, autofill, mobile keyboards, and user settings. Recreating all of that is expensive.

Custom controls can be justified, but only when they solve a real problem and the team is ready to own the behavior. The decision needs a spec, tests, and maintenance plan.

The right question is not can we build it. It is whether the custom version improves the product enough to justify the risk.
keyPoints: Ask what user or brand outcome cannot be achieved by styling or composing native controls.
Estimate the full cost: keyboard behavior, screen readers, mobile input, validation, autofill, high contrast, localization, browser changes, and testing.
Prefer native elements or proven accessible library primitives for critical controls.
Approve custom controls only with a complete interaction specification, ownership, and cross-assistive-technology test plan.
Visual uniqueness should not create lower usability or permanent maintenance burden.

blocks.question: A design team proposes a completely custom control for every native form element. How do you evaluate it?
blocks.answer:
I would start by asking what user or brand outcome requires a fully custom control. If native controls can be styled or composed to meet the need, that is usually the better path.

Custom form controls are not just visuals. They need keyboard behavior, screen-reader support, mobile input behavior, validation, autofill, focus, disabled state, high contrast, localization, and browser compatibility.

For critical controls, I prefer native elements or proven accessible primitives. They carry years of platform behavior that is easy to underestimate.

If the team still wants a custom control, I would require a complete interaction spec. That includes keyboard rules, labels and announcements, touch behavior, error handling, and edge cases.

I would also require ownership and a test plan across assistive technologies and supported browsers. A custom control is a long-term maintenance commitment.

Visual uniqueness is not enough if it makes the product harder to use or expensive to keep correct.
